## What is omeprazole?
Omeprazole is used to treat excess stomach acid in conditions such as stomach ulcers, heartburn or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), active duodenal ulcer, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome and erosive esophagitis.
Omeprazole may also be given together with antibiotics to treat gastric ulcers caused by infection with Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), in adult patients.
Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that works by blocking the acid pump in your stomach, reducing how much acid it makes and giving irritated or damaged tissue a chance to heal.
Omeprazole brand names are Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, and generic brands are available.
Omeprazole is available over the counter (OTC) and as a prescription medication.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## How does metformin help PCOS?
Metformin is prescribed to manage polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) because it improves how the body responds to insulin. PCOS affects about 1 in 10 women of reproductive age and is often marked by insulin resistance, in which the body doesn't respond well to insulin, prompting the pancreas to produce more. This excess insulin drives up androgen (male hormone) production, worsening symptoms like irregular periods, infertility, acne, and excess hair growth. Metformin helps by lowering insulin levels, decreasing the liver's glucose production, improving glucose uptake by muscles, and reducing circulating androgen levels as well, which can support more regular ovulation and menstrual cycles.
Although metformin is not FDA-approved to treat PCOS, it's widely prescribed as an off-label treatment, particularly for those with insulin resistance or fertility difficulties, and it's backed by extensive research and clinical guidelines. Beyond helping regulate cycles and support ovulation, metformin may also help reduce androgen-related symptoms such as acne and excess hair growth, and can aid with weight management for those affected by PCOS-related weight gain.

## What are the side effects of rosuvastatin?
Common side effects:
The most common side effects may include headache, nausea, muscle aches and pains, weakness, and constipation.
Serious side effects:
Rosuvastatin may cause serious side effects, including:
- Muscle pain, tenderness and weakness (myopathy). Muscle problems, including muscle breakdown, can be serious in some people and rarely cause kidney damage that can lead to death. Tell your doctor right away if: you have unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially if you have a fever or feel more tired than usual, while you take this medicine. you have muscle problems that do not go away even after your doctor has told you to stop taking this medicine. Your doctor may do further tests to diagnose the cause of your muscle problems. Your chances of getting muscle problems are higher if you: are taking certain other medicines while you take rosuvastatin are 65 years of age or older are of Asian descent have thyroid problems (hypothyroidism) that are not controlled have kidney problems are taking higher doses of this medicine
- Liver problems. Your doctor may do blood tests to check your liver before you start taking this medicine and if you have symptoms of liver problems while you are taking it. Call your doctor right away if you have any of the following symptoms of liver problems: feel unusually tired or weak loss of appetite upper belly pain dark urine yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes
- Protein and blood in the urine. Rosuvastatin may cause you to have protein and blood in your urine. If you develop protein or blood in your urine, your doctor may decrease your dose.
- Increase in blood sugar (glucose) levels. Rosuvastatin may cause an increase in your blood sugar levels.
Additional side effects that have been reported with rosuvastatin include abdominal pain, dizziness, memory loss and confusion.
Tell your doctor if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away.
These are not all the possible side effects. For more information, ask your doctor or pharmacist.
Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Cyclobenzaprine dosage
The usual cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm is 5 mg three times a day, which may be increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed. The maximum dose is 30 mg per day. Cyclobenzaprine is taken for a maximum of 2 to 3 weeks. 1
Cyclobenzaprine dosage chart:
Immediate-release tablets: the usual starting dose is 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day based on your response. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver problems, treatment should start at 5 mg and be increased slowly, if at all. The tablets are not recommended with moderate to severe liver impairment. 1
Amrix extended-release capsules: the recommended dose is 15 mg once daily for most adults; some people may need 30 mg once daily (one 30 mg capsule or two 15 mg capsules). Amrix is not recommended in adults 65 and older, or in anyone with liver impairment of any severity. 2
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia): The recommended starting dose of Tonmya is 2.8 mg (1 sublingual tablet) once daily at bedtime for the first 14 days, then increases to the target dose of 5.6 mg (2 sublingual tablets) once daily at bedtime from day 15 onward. The maximum is 5.6 mg once daily. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver impairment, the maximum is 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime, and Tonmya is not recommended with moderate or severe liver impairment. 3
Product | Usual adult dose | Maximum dose | How long
Immediate-release tablets, formerly sold as Flexeril (adults and children 15 and older) | 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed | 30 mg per day (10 mg three times a day) | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Amrix extended-release capsules | 15 mg once daily | 30 mg once daily | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia) | 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime for 14 days, then 5.6 mg once daily at bedtime | 5.6 mg once daily | Ongoing, as directed
1,2,3
Can I take 2 cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at the same time?:
No. Do not take two cyclobenzaprine 10 mg tablets at once. The maximum recommended single dose of the immediate-release tablet is 10 mg, taken up to three times a day. Taking 20 mg at one time increases the risk of side effects such as severe drowsiness and fast heart rate, and in overdose cyclobenzaprine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, without providing better muscle spasm relief. If your dose is not controlling your symptoms, talk with your doctor rather than doubling up. 1
How often can you take cyclobenzaprine?:
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day. Amrix extended-release capsules and Tonmya sublingual tablets are taken once a day. Do not take extra doses between scheduled doses. 1,2,3
How long does cyclobenzaprine take to work, and how long does it last?:
In clinical trials of the immediate-release tablets, the muscle relaxant effect was measurable within the first several days, with significant improvement in muscle spasm and pain by day 3 or 4 of treatment. 1
With Amrix extended-release capsules, the drug is first detectable in the blood about 1.5 hours after a dose, with peak levels at 7 to 8 hours, and one daily dose provides day-long coverage. 2
How long does cyclobenzaprine stay in your system?:
Cyclobenzaprine stays in your system for about 3 to 7 days after your last dose. It has a half-life of around 18 hours for the immediate-release tablets, and a drug takes 4 to 5 half-lives to clear from the body. 1
The once-daily forms last longer: the half-life is about 32 hours for Amrix extended-release capsules and about 36 hours for Tonmya sublingual tablets, so these can take a week or more to fully clear. Cyclobenzaprine also stays in the body longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, in whom blood levels run higher. 1,2,3
Does cyclobenzaprine show up on a drug test?:
No, cyclobenzaprine does not usually show up on a drug test, as it is not a controlled substance and it is not one of the five substances (amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine) required on standard federal workplace drug tests. 3,5
However, cyclobenzaprine has a similar structure to tricyclic antidepressants, and it is a recognized cause of false positive results on tricyclic antidepressant immunoassays, including urine immunoassays. Tests for tricyclic antidepressants are not part of routine drugs-of-abuse screening. 5
If you take cyclobenzaprine and need a drug test, tell the testing provider what medicines you take. A screening result is only presumptive, and a confirmatory laboratory test such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry can tell cyclobenzaprine apart from a tricyclic antidepressant. 5

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use atorvastatin if you are allergic to it, or if you have liver failure or cirrhosis.
To make sure atorvastatin is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- muscle pain or weakness;
- diabetes;
- stroke;
- a thyroid disorder;
- a habit of drinking more than 2 alcoholic beverages per day; or
- kidney disease.
Atorvastatin can cause the breakdown of muscle tissue, which can lead to kidney failure. This happens more often in women, in older adults, or people who have kidney disease or poorly controlled hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid).
Pregnancy:
Tell your healthcare professional if you are pregnant, or plan to become pregnant, or become pregnant. Atorvastatin may harm your unborn baby. If you become pregnant, stop taking atorvastatin and call your healthcare provider right away.
Breastfeeding:
Tell your healthcare professional if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed. You and your healthcare provider should decide if you will take this medicine or breastfeed. You should not take atorvastatin if you breastfeed. Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed your baby if you take LIPITOR.

## What is rosuvastatin used for?
Rosuvastatin is used:
- to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular (CV) events, such as death from cardiovascular disease, heart attack, stroke, or the need for procedures to improve blood flow to the heart called arterial revascularization, in adults at increased risk for these events.

## Semaglutide side effects
Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.
Stomach or gastrointestinal side effects are common, but they tend to be mild and clear up in a few weeks and usually will not interfere with long-term treatment. Stomach side effects can be more common with higher doses.
Tips for managing stomach side effects:
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
- Eat more slowly
- Eat smaller meals
- Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
- Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
- Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
- Do not lie down right after eating
- Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
- If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach
- Ryebelsus is not recommended in patients with severe gastroparesis.
Tips for managing low blood sugar levels (hypoglycemia) side effects:
- Test blood sugar levels regularly if you are also taking diabetic medicines, including insulin or sulphonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide/glyburide, glipizide, and gliclazide) and when you increase your semaglutide dose.
- Your prescriber might reduce your dose of insulin or sulphonylureas if needed to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia
- Symptoms of low blood sugar levels include:
- Treatment for hypoglycemia
- Severe hypoglycemia may require a glucagon injection.
Serious semaglutide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives, itching, dizziness, fast heartbeats, difficulty breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- vision changes;
- unusual mood changes, thoughts about hurting yourself;
- pounding heartbeats or fluttering in your chest;
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
- signs of a thyroid tumor - swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, feeling short of breath;
- symptoms of pancreatitis - severe pain in your upper stomach spreading to your back, nausea with or without vomiting, fast heart rate;
- gallbladder problems - upper stomach pain, fever, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes);
- low blood sugar - headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
- kidney problems - swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath; or
- stomach flu symptoms - stomach cramps, vomiting, loss of appetite, diarrhea (may be watery or bloody); or severe stomach problems like severe constipation, fecal impaction, or intestinal obstruction.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is Flonase?
Flonase is a nasal spray containing fluticasone propionate. Fluticasone propionate is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation in the lining of the nose.
Flonase Nasal Spray is used to treat nasal congestion, sneezing, runny nose, and itchy or watery eyes caused by seasonal or year-round allergies.
Flonase Allergy Relief is for use in adults and children who are at least 4 years old and is available without a prescription. Children's Flonase Allergy Relief contains the same medicine and is also for ages 4 and older.
Flonase Sensimist contains fluticasone furoate rather than fluticasone propionate and is approved for use in adults and children 2 years of age and older. Children's Flonase Sensimist is also for ages 2 and older. In Flonase Sensimist labeling, relief of itchy, watery eyes applies to ages 12 and older.
The brand-name prescription version of Flonase nasal spray has been discontinued in the United States. Generic fluticasone propionate nasal spray is still available by prescription, and over-the-counter Flonase products and store brands remain on the market.
Some products sold under the Flonase brand name are not nasal sprays and do not contain fluticasone. Flonase Headache & Allergy Relief caplets contain acetaminophen, chlorpheniramine, and phenylephrine, and Flonase Nighttime Allergy Relief tablets contain triprolidine. Check the active ingredients on the carton before use.

## Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
Metoprolol crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.
Studies published to date have not shown a link between metoprolol taken in pregnancy and major birth defects or miscarriage. Reports on growth restriction, early birth, and death around the time of birth have been inconsistent, and those studies have limitations that make them hard to interpret. Untreated high blood pressure and untreated heart failure in pregnancy carry their own serious risks for both mother and baby.
Babies born to mothers taking metoprolol may have low blood pressure, low blood sugar, a slow heartbeat, or slow breathing, so they are watched after birth.
The amount of metoprolol a breastfed baby receives is estimated at 0.05 mg to under 1 mg a day, which is about 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose. No side effects in breastfed babies have been identified. Babies are still monitored for a slow heartbeat and for signs such as unusual sleepiness.

## Warnings
You should not use potassium chloride if you have high levels of potassium in your blood (hyperkalemia), or if you also take a "potassium-sparing" diuretic.
To be sure potassium chloride is helping your condition, your blood may need to be tested often. Your heart rate may also be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG) to measure electrical activity of the heart. This test will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium. Do not miss any scheduled appointments.
Serious side effects of potassium include uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or limp feeling, severe stomach pain, and numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or mouth.
Do not stop taking this medicine without first talking to your doctor. If you stop taking this medicine suddenly, your condition may become worse.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on an extended-release tablet or capsule. Swallow the pill whole unless your doctor or pharmacist tells you your specific tablet can be broken. Crushing or chewing the pill may cause too much of the drug to be released at one time. Sucking on a tablet can irritate your mouth or throat. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.

## Metformin side effects
Common side effects:
Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. These side effects occurred in 5% or more of patients in the US clinical trial of using metformin for type 2 diabetic patients. In the same study, 6% of patients discontinued metformin due to diarrhea.
Less common side effects were abnormal stools, hypoglycemia, myalgia, lightheadedness, dyspnea, nail disorder, rash, increased sweating, taste disorder, chest discomfort, chills, flu syndrome, flushing, and palpitation, which occurred between 1% and less than 5% of patients.
Taking your medicine with meals can help reduce these side effects, and you may find the slow-release tablets reduce gastric side effects. Tell your doctor if the side effects bother you a lot, last for more than a few weeks, come back after they've gone away, or start later in therapy. You may need a lower dose or need to stop taking the medicine for a short period or for good.
Metformin rarely causes hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) by itself. However, hypoglycemia can happen if you do not eat enough, if you drink alcohol, or if you take other medicines to lower blood sugar.
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to metformin: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
This medicine can rarely cause patients to develop lactic acidosis, which can be fatal. See the “Warnings - Boxed Warning” for more details.
Call your doctor at once if you have signs of liver problems, such as upper stomach pain, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, or yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice).

## Gabapentin side effects
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
Other common gabapentin side effects may include:
- unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
- nausea or vomiting
- headache
- trouble speaking
- blurred or double vision
- tremor
- signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body. Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.
Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking this medicine and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol. A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.
Some side effects are more likely in children taking gabapentin. Call your doctor if the child has behavior changes, memory problems, trouble concentrating, or is restless, hostile, or aggressive.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- drowsiness, dizziness, or weakness
- problems with balance or muscle movement
- increased seizures
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is amoxicillin?
Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections such as tonsillitis, bronchitis, sinusitis, pneumonia, and infections of the ear, nose, throat, skin, or urinary tract.
Amoxicillin clavulanate is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanate potassium. The amoxicillin fights bacteria, and the clavulanate potassium helps prevent certain bacteria from becoming resistant to amoxicillin.
Amoxicillin is also sometimes used together with another antibiotic called clarithromycin (Biaxin) to treat stomach ulcers caused by Helicobacter pylori infection. This combination is sometimes used with a stomach acid reducer called lansoprazole (Prevacid).
Amoxicillin 500mg and 250mg are available as tablets or capsules and as an oral suspension. Many brands and forms of amoxicillin are available, and not all brands are listed on this leaflet.

Tell your doctor about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. ## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Before taking this medicine
Meloxicam can increase your risk of a fatal heart attack or stroke. Do not use this medicine just before or after heart bypass surgery (coronary artery bypass graft, or CABG). Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal.
Meloxicam may also cause stomach or intestinal bleeding, which can be fatal. These conditions can occur without warning while you are using this medicine, especially in older adults.
You should not use meloxicam if you are allergic to it, or if you have ever had an asthma attack or severe allergic reaction after taking aspirin or an NSAID.
To make sure meloxicam is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- heart disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or if you smoke;
- a heart attack, stroke, or blood clot;
- ulcers or stomach bleeding;
- asthma;
- kidney disease (or if you are on dialysis);
- liver disease; or
- fluid retention
- are pregnant or planning a pregnancy
- are breastfeeding or intending to breastfeed.
Meloxicam is not approved for use by anyone younger than 2 years old.
Pregnancy:
If you are pregnant, you should not take meloxicam unless your doctor tells you to. Taking an NSAID at about 20 weeks of pregnancy or later may harm your unborn baby. If you need to take this medicine for more than 2 days when you are between 20 and 30 weeks of pregnancy, your doctor may need to monitor the amount of fluid around your baby. You should not take meloxicam after about 30 weeks of pregnancy.
Planning a pregnancy:
Meloxicam may cause a delay in ovulation (the release of an egg from an ovary). You should not take this medicine if you are undergoing fertility treatment or are otherwise trying to get pregnant.
Breastfeeding:
Ask a doctor if it is safe to breastfeed while using this medicine.

evidence:
## How should I use insulin glargine?
Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Use the medicine exactly as directed. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you don't understand how to use an injection.
Prepare an injection only when you are ready to give it. Do not use it if the medicine looks cloudy, has changed colors, or has particles in it.
Insulin glargine is injected under the skin, using a syringe or insulin pen, once per day at the same time of day.
Insulin can be injected into your upper legs (thighs), upper arms, or stomach area (abdomen). Do not inject into the same place two times in a row. Avoid injecting into skin that is damaged, tender, bruised, pitted, thickened, scaly, or has a scar or hard lump.
When treating type 1 diabetes, use your short-acting insulin before meals as directed by your doctor.
Insulin glargine must not be given with an insulin pump or mixed with other insulins. Do not inject insulin glargine into a vein or a muscle.
Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of this medicine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
If you use an injection pen, use only the injection pen that comes with insulin glargine. Attach a new needle before each use. Do not transfer the insulin from the pen into a syringe.
Never share an injection pen, even if you changed the needle. Sharing these devices can pass infections from person to person.
Blood sugar can be affected by stress, illness, surgery, exercise, alcohol use, or skipping meals.
Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can make you feel very hungry, dizzy, irritable, or shaky. To quickly treat hypoglycemia, eat or drink hard candy, crackers, raisins, fruit juice, or non-diet soda. Your doctor may prescribe glucagon injections in case of severe hypoglycemia.
Tell your doctor if you have frequent symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia), such as increased thirst or urination. Ask your doctor before changing your medication dosage.
Wear a medical alert tag or carry an ID card to let others know you have diabetes.

## Warnings
You should not take carvedilol if you have asthma, bronchitis, emphysema, severe liver disease, severe heart failure requiring certain IV medications, or a serious heart condition such as heart block, "sick sinus syndrome," or slow heart rate (unless you have a pacemaker).
Avoid drinking alcohol within 2 hours before or after taking extended-release carvedilol (Coreg CR). Also avoid taking medicines or other products that might contain alcohol. Alcohol may cause the carvedilol in Coreg CR to be released too quickly into the body.

## Warnings
Cetirizine can cause side effects that may impair your thinking or reactions. Be careful if you drive or do anything that requires you to be awake and alert. Avoid drinking alcohol. It can increase some of the side effects of cetirizine.
Tell your doctor if you regularly use other medicines that make you sleepy (such as other cold or allergy medicine, narcotic pain medicine, sleeping pills, muscle relaxers, and medicine for seizures, depression, or anxiety). They can add to sleepiness caused by cetirizine.
Call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve, if they get worse, or if you also have a fever.
If you are taking cetirizine for hives, get emergency medical help immediately if you have trouble swallowing, dizziness, swelling of the tongue or around the mouth, trouble speaking, drooling, or wheezing. Cetirizine is not a substitute for an epinephrine injector. Do not use cetirizine to prevent hives from known causes such as foods, insect stings, or medicines. Call your doctor if your hives do not improve after 3 days, if they last more than 6 weeks, or if they are an unusual color, look bruised or blistered, or do not itch.
Rarely, some people have reported severe itching when stopping cetirizine after daily, long-term use of at least a few months or several years. If you experience widespread, severe itching on stopping this medication, contact your healthcare provider.

## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is losartan?
Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.
Losartan is also used to decrease the risk of stroke in people who have high blood pressure and a heart condition called left ventricular hypertrophy (enlargement of the walls of the left side of the heart).

## Fluoxetine Dosing Information
Fluoxetine (Prozac) is taken orally, and your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition, age, and response to treatment. Always follow your doctor's instructions, do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine without speaking to them first.
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD):
Adults: Treatment typically starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning. Your doctor may increase the dose after several weeks if needed. The maximum dose is 80 mg/day.
Children and adolescents (aged 8 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg or 20 mg per day. In lower-weight children, the starting dose and target dose may remain at 10 mg/day.
With all patients, the full effect of fluoxetine for depression may take 4 weeks or longer.
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD):
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning and may be increased after several weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement. The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day. Full therapeutic effect may take 5 weeks or longer.
Adolescents and higher-weight children (aged 7 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after 2 weeks. Additional dose increases may be considered after several more weeks if insufficient clinical improvement is observed. The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day.
Lower-weight children: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day with dose increases after several more weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement. The recommended dose range of 20 mg to 30 mg per day, although experience with daily doses greater than 20 mg is very minimal,
Bulimia Nervosa:
Adult dose: The recommended dose is 60 mg once daily in the morning. Your doctor may gradually increase your dose to this level over several days. Clinical trials showed that the 60 mg dose was effective in reducing binge-eating and purging behaviors.
Panic Disorder:
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after one week. Your doctor may adjust the dose after several weeks if needed. Clinical trials used a dose range of 10 mg/day to 60 mg/day, but the most commonly used dose in clinical trials was 20 mg/day.
General Dosing Notes:
- Fluoxetine is usually taken in the morning to minimize the risk of sleep disturbances
- It may take several weeks to feel the full benefit of fluoxetine, do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first
- Your doctor will periodically reassess whether you need to continue treatment
- Older adults may need a lower dose or may take fluoxetine less frequently than younger adults
- People with liver problems may also require a lower or less frequent dose
- If you have other medical conditions or take multiple medications, your doctor may need to adjust your fluoxetine dose accordingly

## What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.
No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.
This list is not complete, and many other medicines may interact with tamsulosin. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

## What is allopurinol?
Allopurinol belongs to a class of medications called xanthine oxidase inhibitors. It works by reducing the production of uric acid in the body. High levels of uric acid may cause gout attacks or kidney stones.
Allopurinol is used to treat gout (a type of arthritis in which uric acid, a naturally occurring substance in the body, builds up in the joints and causes sudden attacks of redness, swelling, pain, and heat in one or more joints). Allopurinol is used to prevent gout attacks, not to treat them once they occur. Allopurinol does not need to be stopped during an acute flare.
Allopurinol is also used to treat high levels of uric acid that builds up in the blood as tumors break down in people with certain types of cancer who are being treated with chemotherapy medications. It is also used to treat kidney stones that have come back in people who have high levels of uric acid in their urine.

## How long does omeprazole take to work?
Omeprazole usually takes 1 to 4 days of once-daily dosing to reach its full effect, and some people get complete relief of their symptoms within 24 hours. It begins reducing stomach acid within about 1 hour of the first dose, but it is not designed to relieve heartburn right away.
What to expect after you start taking omeprazole:
- Within 1 hour: omeprazole starts to reduce acid production in your stomach
- Around 2 hours: a single dose reaches its strongest acid-lowering effect
- Within 24 hours: some people get complete relief of their symptoms
- 1 to 4 days: most people feel the full benefit
- About 4 days: the acid-lowering effect reaches its maximum with once-daily dosing
How fast does omeprazole start working?:
Omeprazole starts working within about 1 hour, and a single dose has its strongest effect at around 2 hours. This is when the medicine begins lowering acid production, which is not the same as when your heartburn or acid reflux symptoms stop.
Omeprazole does not work immediately on symptoms you are already feeling. It is a proton pump inhibitor (PPI), which means it reduces how much acid your stomach makes rather than neutralizing acid that is already there.

## What is amlodipine?
Amlodipine besylate is a prescription medicine used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent certain types of angina (chest pain). It belongs to a class of medications called calcium channel blockers.
Amlodipine besylate works by relaxing and widening the blood vessels, so blood flows more easily which improves blood pressure.
Amlodipine besylate controls angina chest pain by increasing the supply of blood to the heart. If taken regularly, this medicine controls chest pain, but it does not stop chest pain once it starts. Your doctor may prescribe a different medication to take when you have chest pain.
Amlodipine is also used alone or in combination with other medicines to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) in adults and children at least 6 years old. Lowering blood pressure may lower your risk of a stroke or heart attack.
Amlodipine besylate is available as:
- Amlodipine 5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 10 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 2.5 mg tablets (Norvasc)
- Amlodipine 1 mg/mL solution (Norliqva)

## Boxed warning: suicidal thoughts and behaviors
Sertraline carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious type of warning. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teenagers, and young adults in short-term studies.
In pooled analyses of placebo-controlled antidepressant trials covering about 77,000 adults and more than 4,500 children and teenagers, the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in people aged 24 and under was higher with an antidepressant than with placebo. The risk varied considerably between different antidepressants, and it also varied by condition, with the highest rate in people being treated for depression. The difference between antidepressant and placebo, per 1,000 patients treated, was:
Age (years) | Difference compared with placebo
Under 18 | 14 more patients with suicidal thoughts or behaviors
18 to 24 | 5 more patients
25 to 64 | 1 fewer patient
65 and over | 6 fewer patients
It is not known whether this risk continues beyond about four months of treatment. There is good evidence that antidepressants delay depression coming back in adults, and depression itself raises the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors.
Anyone taking sertraline should be watched closely for worsening symptoms and for new or sudden changes in mood, behavior, thoughts, or feelings, especially in the first few months of treatment and whenever the dose is changed. Call your healthcare provider right away, or call 911 in an emergency, if you notice:
- thoughts about suicide or dying, or attempts to harm yourself
- new or worse depression, anxiety, or panic attacks
- feeling agitated, restless, angry, or irritable
- acting aggressive or violent, or acting on dangerous impulses
- trouble sleeping
- a big increase in activity or talking more than is normal for you
- any other unusual change in behavior or mood
Tell family members or caregivers which symptoms to watch for, so they can call your provider if you are not able to.

## Can you take metoprolol during pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
Metoprolol crosses the placenta and passes into breast milk in small amounts. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.
Studies published to date have not shown a link between metoprolol taken in pregnancy and major birth defects or miscarriage. Reports on growth restriction, early birth, and death around the time of birth have been inconsistent, and those studies have limitations that make them hard to interpret. Untreated high blood pressure and untreated heart failure in pregnancy carry their own serious risks for both mother and baby.
Babies born to mothers taking metoprolol may have low blood pressure, low blood sugar, a slow heartbeat, or slow breathing, so they are watched after birth.
The amount of metoprolol a breastfed baby receives is estimated at 0.05 mg to under 1 mg a day, which is about 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose. No side effects in breastfed babies have been identified. Babies are still monitored for a slow heartbeat and for signs such as unusual sleepiness.

## What other drugs will affect tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is broken down in the body mainly by two liver enzymes, CYP3A4 and CYP2D6. Medicines that block these enzymes can raise the amount of tamsulosin in your blood and increase the risk of side effects.
Do not take tamsulosin with:
- strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ketoconazole
- other alpha blockers, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin, silodosin, or terazosin
Use with caution, and tell your doctor if you take:
- moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin
- strong CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as paroxetine, or moderate CYP2D6 inhibitors, such as terbinafine
- cimetidine
- warfarin
- medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension known as PDE5 inhibitors, including avanafil (Stendra), sildenafil (Viagra, Revatio), tadalafil (Adcirca, Cialis), and vardenafil (Levitra). Taking these with tamsulosin can lower blood pressure enough to cause symptoms.
Some of these cautions matter more at the higher 0.8 mg dose than at 0.4 mg. Your doctor will decide what is right for you.
No dose change is needed if you take tamsulosin with nifedipine, atenolol, enalapril, digoxin, theophylline, or furosemide.

## How does atorvastatin work?
Atorvastatin works by selectively blocking HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme the liver uses to produce cholesterol. By slowing this process, it reduces cholesterol production in the liver and increases the number of LDL receptors on liver cells, which helps remove more LDL (“bad”) cholesterol from the bloodstream.
As a result, it lowers overall LDL levels, decreases the number of LDL particles, and improves the body’s ability to clear cholesterol.

## Spironolactone FAQs
Is spironolactone a diuretic?:
Yes. Spironolactone is a diuretic, or water pill, and it belongs to the group called potassium-sparing diuretics. It works by blocking aldosterone, a hormone that makes your kidneys hold onto salt and water. Unlike most water pills, which make you lose potassium, spironolactone makes your body keep potassium in. It is a weaker diuretic than medicines such as furosemide, which is one reason it is often given alongside another water pill rather than instead of one.
Is spironolactone used for acne?:
Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating acne, but doctors sometimes prescribe it off-label for hormonal acne in women. Off-label means a doctor is prescribing a medicine for something other than its approved uses, which is legal and common, but it means the FDA has not reviewed the medicine for that purpose.
The reason it is used this way relates to how spironolactone works. As well as blocking aldosterone, spironolactone attaches to the androgen receptor, the docking point for male hormones such as testosterone. Male hormones increase how much oil the skin produces, and oil production is one factor in acne.
Because acne is not an approved use, there is no FDA-approved dose for it. Any dose is chosen by the prescriber. Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy because it may affect how a male baby develops, which is an important consideration for anyone taking it for a skin condition rather than a heart or kidney condition.
If you are considering spironolactone for acne, this is a conversation to have with a doctor or dermatologist who can review your full medical history, since spironolactone still carries the same risk of raising your potassium level, whatever it is prescribed for.
Does spironolactone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is not a recognized side effect of spironolactone, and it is not listed in the medicine's official prescribing information. Spironolactone is a diuretic, so it usually causes a small drop in weight in the first week or two as your body sheds extra fluid.
If you are gaining weight while taking it, it is worth telling your doctor rather than assuming the medicine is to blame. Rapid weight gain with swelling in your ankles or legs or shortness of breath can be a sign of fluid building up, which may mean the condition being treated needs a closer look. Slower weight gain is more often down to appetite, activity, or another medicine.
Does spironolactone cause hair loss?:
Hair thinning, known as alopecia, is listed as a possible side effect of spironolactone, though how often it happens is not known. It is reported far less often than breast tenderness or breast growth.
The picture is complicated because spironolactone is also prescribed off label for hair loss in women, on the basis that blocking male hormones may help with hormone-related thinning. Spironolactone is not approved by the FDA for treating hair loss. If your hair is thinning while you take it, speak to your doctor, since there are several possible causes worth ruling out.
How long does it take for spironolactone to work?:
It depends what you are taking it for. Spironolactone reaches its highest level in your blood in about 2 to 3 hours, and its active breakdown product peaks at around 4 hours, so it starts having an effect on your kidneys the same day.
The results you notice take longer. For fluid build-up, spironolactone is given for at least five days before the dose is increased, because that is how long the full effect takes to show. For high blood pressure, the dose is adjusted at two-week intervals, so give it a couple of weeks before judging it. For heart failure, the benefit is a lower risk of being admitted to hospital and living longer, which is not something you feel week to week.
How long does spironolactone stay in your system?:
Spironolactone itself leaves your blood very quickly, with a half-life of about 1.4 hours, meaning half of it is gone in that time. Its active breakdown products last much longer, with half-lives of roughly 14 to 17 hours. Because of those, the effect of a dose carries on well after the spironolactone itself has gone, and it takes a few days for the medicine to clear fully after you stop. Clearance is slower if you have cirrhosis.
Is spironolactone a blood thinner?:
No. Spironolactone is not a blood thinner. It does not affect blood clotting and it is not used to prevent clots or strokes in the way that warfarin, apixaban, or aspirin are. It is a diuretic that lowers blood pressure and reduces fluid build-up.
Spironolactone does interact with some blood thinners indirectly. Heparin and low molecular weight heparin can raise potassium, so taking them with spironolactone increases the risk of a high potassium level.
Can I stop taking spironolactone suddenly?:
Spironolactone does not cause withdrawal symptoms and does not need to be tapered the way a steroid does. Even so, do not stop it without speaking to your doctor. Stopping it can allow fluid to build up again, your blood pressure to rise, or your heart failure to worsen, and if you are taking it for heart failure it is one of the medicines shown to help people live longer. If side effects are the reason you want to stop, a dose change or a different medicine may be an option.
Can you take spironolactone at night?:
There is no fixed time of day for spironolactone. What matters more is that you take it at the same time each day and always the same way with regard to food, since food changes how much you absorb. Many people prefer the morning because spironolactone makes you pass more urine, and a late dose can mean getting up in the night. If a nighttime dose suits you better, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you drink alcohol while taking spironolactone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and spironolactone, but drinking is best kept modest. Both can lower your blood pressure and make you light-headed, so together they raise the chance of feeling dizzy or faint, particularly when you stand up. Alcohol is also a problem in its own right if you are taking spironolactone for liver disease. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for your situation.
Can you take spironolactone while pregnant?:
Spironolactone is generally avoided in pregnancy. It blocks the action of male hormones, and in animal studies male offspring exposed before birth developed abnormally. Human data are limited and have not shown a clear increase in birth defects, but the concern is enough that the manufacturer advises avoiding it or discussing the potential risk to a male baby.
Do not stop spironolactone on your own if you find out you are pregnant. Tell your doctor straight away, because untreated heart failure, cirrhosis, and high blood pressure also carry serious risks in pregnancy and your treatment will need to be changed carefully.
Does spironolactone cause constipation?:
Constipation is not a listed side effect of spironolactone. The digestive side effects that have been reported are the opposite, including diarrhea and stomach cramping, along with nausea, vomiting, and indigestion. If you are constipated while taking spironolactone, another cause is more likely, and it is worth mentioning to your pharmacist, who can check the rest of your medicines.
Is 200 mg of spironolactone too much?:
It depends on the reason you are taking it. For fluid build-up, the approved dose range goes up to 200 mg a day, and for primary hyperaldosteronism it goes up to 400 mg a day, so 200 mg is within the licensed range for both.
For high blood pressure it would be above the usual range, since doses over 100 mg a day do not lower blood pressure any further. For heart failure the usual dose is 25 mg to 50 mg a day, so 200 mg would be well above what is normally used. Higher doses also carry a greater risk of high potassium and of breast growth in men. If your dose seems high for your condition, ask your prescriber rather than adjusting it yourself.
Why is spironolactone described as a high-risk medicine?:
The main reason is the risk of a high potassium level, which can cause a dangerous change in your heart rhythm and often gives no warning symptoms. The risk rises if your kidneys do not work well or if you take other medicines that raise potassium, and several very common medicines do, including ibuprofen and some blood pressure tablets.
This risk is manageable, which is why blood tests are built into treatment. Your potassium should be checked within a week of starting spironolactone or changing your dose, and regularly after that. Spironolactone also needs care in pregnancy and in people with liver disease.

## Hydrochlorothiazide FAQ
Does hydrochlorothiazide cause weight loss?:
Hydrochlorothiazide is not a weight loss medicine. Some people see the number on the scales drop in the first days or weeks of treatment, but this is extra fluid leaving the body rather than any loss of body fat, and it levels off. Do not take hydrochlorothiazide to lose weight.
Can you drink alcohol while taking hydrochlorothiazide?:
Alcohol can make the drop in blood pressure that happens when you stand up worse, which may leave you feeling dizzy or faint. The same applies to barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. Tell your doctor how much you drink so they can advise you.
Does hydrochlorothiazide lower your potassium?:
Yes. Hydrochlorothiazide can lower blood potassium (hypokalemia), and this is more likely at higher doses, when fluid is lost quickly, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after taking the medicine for a long time. Your doctor will check your potassium with blood tests. Tell them if you have muscle cramps, unusual weakness or tiredness, or an irregular heartbeat.
Should you eat more potassium while taking hydrochlorothiazide?:
Only if your doctor tells you to. Low potassium can sometimes be managed with potassium-rich foods, a potassium supplement, or a different type of diuretic that holds on to potassium. Do not start any of these yourself, because too much potassium can also be harmful, and some people on hydrochlorothiazide do not need extra potassium at all.
Is hydrochlorothiazide 12.5mg enough?:

## Spironolactone side effects
Reported spironolactone side effects:
Reported spironolactone side effects include breast and nipple pain in both men and women, a lower sex drive, trouble getting or keeping an erection, irregular or missed periods, bleeding after menopause, dizziness, headache, drowsiness, feeling sluggish, leg cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, indigestion, hair thinning, and itching.
The most common side effect of spironolactone is breast growth in men, known as gynecomastia. In the main heart failure study, about 9 in 100 men taking an average of 26 mg a day developed it. The chance goes up on higher doses. It can start anywhere from one or two months into treatment to more than a year later, and it usually goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Several of these effects are dose-related, so they are more likely on higher doses, and many settle after the dose is lowered or the medicine is stopped. How often most of them happen is not known, because they come from reports gathered after the medicine was approved rather than from counted numbers in trials.
Serious spironolactone side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to spironolactone: hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of a high potassium level (hyperkalemia), such as muscle weakness or a heavy feeling in your legs, a slow or uneven heartbeat, numbness or tingling in your hands, feet, or lips, nausea, or feeling restless and on edge;
- a light-headed feeling like you might pass out, which can be a sign you have low blood pressure (hypotension)
- little or no urination, or swelling in your ankles, hands, or feet, which can be signs your kidneys are struggling (worsening renal function);
- signs of a low sodium level, such as confusion, severe weakness, muscle pain or cramps, feeling unsteady, or slurred speech;
- severe or ongoing vomiting or diarrhea, since losing too much fluid and salt can send your blood pressure and kidney function the wrong way;
- a skin rash that spreads or blisters, peeling skin, sores in your mouth, or a rash with a fever and swollen glands, which can be signs of a rare but serious skin reaction;
- yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, or pain in your upper stomach, which can be signs of a liver problem;
- a fever, sore throat, or unusual bruising or bleeding, which can be signs of a problem with your blood cells; or
- new confusion, unsteadiness, or extreme drowsiness if you have liver disease, since spironolactone can make brain function worse in people with cirrhosis.
Spironolactone side effects in men:
Men are most likely to notice effects linked to spironolactone blocking male hormones. These include breast growth and breast tenderness, a lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. Breast growth is dose related, so tell your doctor early rather than waiting, since a lower dose or a different medicine may be an option.
Spironolactone side effects in women:
Women may notice irregular periods, missed periods, breast tenderness, or bleeding after menopause. Some women also notice patchy darkening of the skin on the face. Report any unexpected bleeding after menopause to your doctor so it can be checked properly rather than assumed to be a side effect.
Long-term spironolactone side effects:
The main long-term concerns with spironolactone are chemical rather than something you would feel. Over time it can push your potassium too high, and it can also lower your sodium, magnesium, and calcium, raise your blood sugar, and raise your uric acid, which occasionally brings on gout. This is why you need regular blood tests for as long as you take it, not just at the start.
In animal studies, spironolactone given at high doses over long periods caused tumors in rats, mainly in hormone-producing glands and the liver. No increase in tumors was seen at the lower doses tested, which were still around five times the highest recommended human dose when adjusted for body size. Whether this happens in people is not known.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Dosing information
Usual adult dose for edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and chronic renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome):
Oral: initial dose 20 to 80 mg orally once. This may be repeated at the same dose or increased by 20 or 40 mg no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose, until the desired diuretic effect has been obtained.
Maintenance dose: administer the dose that provided the desired diuretic effect once or twice a day (for example, at 8 am and 2 pm).
Comments: edema may be most efficiently and safely mobilized by giving this drug on 2 to 4 consecutive days each week. When doses greater than 80 mg/day are given for prolonged periods, careful clinical observation and laboratory monitoring are particularly advisable.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (ReadyFlow autoinjector):
- 80 mg of furosemide given subcutaneously in about 10 seconds.
Usual Furoscix adult and pediatric 43 kg and above dose (On-Body Infusor):
- 30 mg of furosemide over the first hour, then 12.5 mg per hour for the subsequent 4 hours. This dose is delivered automatically by the On-Body Infusor.
- In children weighing at least 43 kg, the device must be applied by a healthcare provider or adult caregiver.
Furoscix is not for chronic use and should be replaced with oral diuretics as soon as practical. People with significantly reduced kidney function may need additional diuretic therapy, because both Furoscix devices deliver a fixed 80 mg dose.
Usual adult furosemide dose for pulmonary edema:
IV: 40 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes. If a satisfactory response does not occur within one hour, this may be increased to 80 mg IV slowly over 1 to 2 minutes.
Use: adjunctive therapy in acute pulmonary edema. IV administration is indicated when a rapid onset of diuresis is desired.
Usual adult furosemide dose for hypertension:
Oral: initial dose 80 mg/day, usually divided into 40 mg orally twice a day.
Use: treatment of hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents.
Usual pediatric furosemide oral dose for edema:
Initial dose: 2 mg/kg orally once. If the diuretic response to the initial dose is not satisfactory, this may be increased by 1 or 2 mg/kg, given no sooner than 6 to 8 hours after the previous dose. Doses greater than 6 mg/kg body weight are not recommended.
Maintenance dose: adjust to the minimum effective dose.
Use: treatment of edema associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver and renal disease, including the nephrotic syndrome, especially when an agent with greater diuretic potential is desired.

## What is Flonase?
Flonase is a nasal spray containing fluticasone propionate. Fluticasone propionate is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation in the lining of the nose.
Flonase Nasal Spray is used to treat nasal congestion, sneezing, runny nose, and itchy or watery eyes caused by seasonal or year-round allergies.
Flonase Allergy Relief is for use in adults and children who are at least 4 years old and is available without a prescription. Children's Flonase Allergy Relief contains the same medicine and is also for ages 4 and older.
Flonase Sensimist contains fluticasone furoate rather than fluticasone propionate and is approved for use in adults and children 2 years of age and older. Children's Flonase Sensimist is also for ages 2 and older. In Flonase Sensimist labeling, relief of itchy, watery eyes applies to ages 12 and older.
The brand-name prescription version of Flonase nasal spray has been discontinued in the United States. Generic fluticasone propionate nasal spray is still available by prescription, and over-the-counter Flonase products and store brands remain on the market.
Some products sold under the Flonase brand name are not nasal sprays and do not contain fluticasone. Flonase Headache & Allergy Relief caplets contain acetaminophen, chlorpheniramine, and phenylephrine, and Flonase Nighttime Allergy Relief tablets contain triprolidine. ## Fluoxetine Side Effects
Like all medications, Prozac can cause side effects. Not everyone experiences them, and many improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts to the medication. Tell your doctor if any side effects bother you or do not go away.
Common Fluoxetine Side Effects:
The most commonly reported side effects of fluoxetine (Prozac) include:
- Nausea
- Trouble sleeping (insomnia)
- Drowsiness or sleepiness
- Anxiety or feeling nervous or on edge
- Trembling or shaking (tremor)
- Excessive sweating
- Loss of appetite
- Diarrhea
- Dry mouth
- Indigestion or upset stomach
- Weakness or fatigue
- Sore throat
- Sinus congestion or infection
- Flu-like symptoms
- Skin rash
- Flushing or feeling of warmth
- Yawning
- Unusual or vivid dreams
- Decreased sex drive
- Difficulty getting or keeping an erection
- Delayed or abnormal ejaculation
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to this medicine (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).
Report any new or worsening symptoms to your doctor, such as mood or behavior changes, anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, hyperactive (mentally or physically), more depressed, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself.
This medicine may cause serious side effects. Call your doctor at once if you have:
- blurred vision, tunnel vision, eye pain or swelling, or seeing halos around lights;
- fast or pounding heartbeats, fluttering in your chest, shortness of breath, and sudden dizziness (like you might pass out);
- low levels of sodium in the body - headache, confusion, slurred speech, severe weakness, vomiting, loss of coordination, feeling unsteady; or
- severe nervous system reaction - very stiff (rigid) muscles, high fever, sweating, confusion, fast or uneven heartbeats, tremors, feeling like you might pass out.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is the usual prednisone dosage?
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

## Cyclobenzaprine dosage
The usual cyclobenzaprine dose for muscle spasm is 5 mg three times a day, which may be increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed. The maximum dose is 30 mg per day. Cyclobenzaprine is taken for a maximum of 2 to 3 weeks. 1
Cyclobenzaprine dosage chart:
Immediate-release tablets: the usual starting dose is 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day based on your response. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver problems, treatment should start at 5 mg and be increased slowly, if at all. The tablets are not recommended with moderate to severe liver impairment. 1
Amrix extended-release capsules: the recommended dose is 15 mg once daily for most adults; some people may need 30 mg once daily (one 30 mg capsule or two 15 mg capsules). Amrix is not recommended in adults 65 and older, or in anyone with liver impairment of any severity. 2
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia): The recommended starting dose of Tonmya is 2.8 mg (1 sublingual tablet) once daily at bedtime for the first 14 days, then increases to the target dose of 5.6 mg (2 sublingual tablets) once daily at bedtime from day 15 onward. The maximum is 5.6 mg once daily. In adults 65 and older and in people with mild liver impairment, the maximum is 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime, and Tonmya is not recommended with moderate or severe liver impairment. 3
Product | Usual adult dose | Maximum dose | How long
Immediate-release tablets, formerly sold as Flexeril (adults and children 15 and older) | 5 mg three times a day, increased to 10 mg three times a day if needed | 30 mg per day (10 mg three times a day) | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Amrix extended-release capsules | 15 mg once daily | 30 mg once daily | Up to 2 to 3 weeks
Tonmya sublingual tablets (fibromyalgia) | 2.8 mg once daily at bedtime for 14 days, then 5.6 mg once daily at bedtime | 5.6 mg once daily | Ongoing, as directed
1,2,3
Can I take 2 cyclobenzaprine 10 mg at the same time?:
No. Do not take two cyclobenzaprine 10 mg tablets at once. The maximum recommended single dose of the immediate-release tablet is 10 mg, taken up to three times a day. Taking 20 mg at one time increases the risk of side effects such as severe drowsiness and fast heart rate, and in overdose cyclobenzaprine can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems, without providing better muscle spasm relief. If your dose is not controlling your symptoms, talk with your doctor rather than doubling up. 1
How often can you take cyclobenzaprine?:
Immediate-release tablets are taken three times a day. Amrix extended-release capsules and Tonmya sublingual tablets are taken once a day. Do not take extra doses between scheduled doses. 1,2,3
How long does cyclobenzaprine take to work, and how long does it last?:
In clinical trials of the immediate-release tablets, the muscle relaxant effect was measurable within the first several days, with significant improvement in muscle spasm and pain by day 3 or 4 of treatment. 1
With Amrix extended-release capsules, the drug is first detectable in the blood about 1.5 hours after a dose, with peak levels at 7 to 8 hours, and one daily dose provides day-long coverage. 2
How long does cyclobenzaprine stay in your system?:
Cyclobenzaprine stays in your system for about 3 to 7 days after your last dose. It has a half-life of around 18 hours for the immediate-release tablets, and a drug takes 4 to 5 half-lives to clear from the body. 1
The once-daily forms last longer: the half-life is about 32 hours for Amrix extended-release capsules and about 36 hours for Tonmya sublingual tablets, so these can take a week or more to fully clear. Cyclobenzaprine also stays in the body longer in older adults and in people with liver problems, in whom blood levels run higher. 1,2,3
Does cyclobenzaprine show up on a drug test?:
No, cyclobenzaprine does not usually show up on a drug test, as it is not a controlled substance and it is not one of the five substances (amphetamines, cannabinoids, cocaine, opiates, and phencyclidine) required on standard federal workplace drug tests. 3,5
However, cyclobenzaprine has a similar structure to tricyclic antidepressants, and it is a recognized cause of false positive results on tricyclic antidepressant immunoassays, including urine immunoassays. Tests for tricyclic antidepressants are not part of routine drugs-of-abuse screening. 5
If you take cyclobenzaprine and need a drug test, tell the testing provider what medicines you take. A screening result is only presumptive, and a confirmatory laboratory test such as gas chromatography-mass spectrometry can tell cyclobenzaprine apart from a tricyclic antidepressant. 5
