## What is lisinopril?
Lisinopril is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children 6 years of age and older.
Lisinopril is also used in adults to treat congestive heart failure and to improve survival after a heart attack.
Lisinopril belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors. It works by decreasing certain chemicals that tighten the blood vessels, so blood flows more smoothly and the heart can pump blood more efficiently.
High blood pressure is a common condition and when not treated, can cause damage to the brain, heart, blood vessels, kidneys, and other parts of the body. Damage to these organs may cause heart disease, a heart attack, heart failure, stroke, kidney failure, loss of vision, and other problems. In addition to taking medication, making lifestyle changes will also help to control your blood pressure. These changes include eating a diet that is low in fat and salt, maintaining a healthy weight, exercising at least 30 minutes most days, not smoking, and using alcohol in moderation.

## What other drugs will affect apixaban?
Sometimes it is not safe to use certain medicines at the same time. Some drugs can affect your blood levels of other drugs you use, which may increase side effects or make the medicines less effective.
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines. Many drugs can affect apixaban, especially:
- a blood thinner or any other medicines to treat or prevent blood clots such as enoxaparin, warfarin, heparin, clopidogrel, dipyridamole, prasugrel, and others;
- an antidepressant; or
- NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) --aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), celecoxib, diclofenac, indomethacin, meloxicam, and others.
This list is not complete and many other drugs may affect apixaban. This includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible drug interactions are listed here.

## What other drugs will affect rosuvastatin?
Tell your doctor about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements. Also tell the doctor who prescribes rosuvastatin if another doctor increases the dose of another medicine you are taking. Rosuvastatin may affect the way other medicines work, and other medicines may affect how rosuvastatin works. Especially tell your doctor if you take:
- coumarin anticoagulants (medicines that prevent blood clots, such as warfarin)
- antacids (medicines you take for heartburn that contain aluminum and magnesium hydroxide)
Taking rosuvastatin with certain medicines may increase the risk of muscle problems. Especially tell your doctor if you take:
- cyclosporine (a medicine for your immune system)
- teriflunomide (a medicine used to treat relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis)
- enasidenib (a medicine used to treat acute myeloid leukemia)
- capmatinib (a medicine for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer)
- fostamatinib (a medicine used to treat low platelet counts)
- febuxostat (a medicine used to treat and prevent high blood levels of uric acid)
- gemfibrozil (a fibric acid medicine for lowering cholesterol)
- tafamidis [used to treat cardiomyopathy (enlarged and thickened heart muscle)]
- anti-viral medicines including certain HIV or hepatitis C virus drugs such as: lopinavir, ritonavir, fosamprenavir, tipranavir, atazanavir, simeprevir combination of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir dasabuvir/ombitasvir/paritaprevir/ritonavir elbasvir/grazoprevir sofosbuvir/velpatasvir glecaprevir/pibrentasvir and all other combinations with ledipasvir including ledipasvir/sofosbuvir
- darolutamide (a medicine for the treatment of prostate cancer)
- regorafenib (a medicine used to treat cancer of the colon and rectum)
- fibric acid derivatives (such as fenofibrate)
- ticagrelor (helps reduce the chance of blood clot formation that can block a blood vessel)
- niacin or nicotinic acid
- colchicine (a medicine used to treat gout)
- belumosudil (used to treat chronic graft-versus-host disease)
- momelotinib (used to treat myelofibrosis, a rare form of blood cancer)
Ask your doctor or pharmacist for a list of these medicines if you are not sure. Know all of the medicines you take. Keep a list of them to show your doctor and pharmacist when you get new medicine.

## How should I take potassium chloride?
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup. If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule. Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet. You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water, or mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food. Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.
Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests. You may not notice any change in your symptoms, but your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride. Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG). Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may include a special diet. Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor. Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.
Potassium-rich foods include: squash, baked potatoes (skin on), spinach, lentils, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, zucchini, kidney or navy beans, raisins, watermelon, orange juice, bananas, cantaloupe, and low-fat milk or yogurt. Consume only the daily amounts recommended by your doctor or nutrition counselor.
Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Keep the medication in a closed container.

## Cyclobenzaprine side effects
The most common cyclobenzaprine side effects are drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Most side effects are mild and settle as your body adjusts, but cyclobenzaprine can occasionally cause serious heart rhythm effects and serotonin syndrome. 1
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Common cyclobenzaprine side effects may include: 1
- drowsiness and tiredness;
- dry mouth;
- dizziness;
- fatigue;
- headache;
- nausea, indigestion, or constipation;
- blurred vision;
- unpleasant taste;
- nervousness or confusion.
In placebo-controlled trials of the immediate-release tablets, side effects were dose-related, occurring more often with 10 mg than with 5 mg: 1
Side effect | Cyclobenzaprine 5 mg | Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg | Placebo
Drowsiness | 29% | 38% | 10%
Dry mouth | 21% | 32% | 7%
Fatigue | 6% | 6% | 3%
Headache | 5% | 5% | 8%
With Amrix, the most common side effects are dry mouth (up to 14% at 30 mg), dizziness, fatigue, constipation, nausea, indigestion, and drowsiness. 2
With Tonmya, because it dissolves under the tongue, the most common side effects involve the mouth: reduced feeling or numbness in the mouth (23%), mouth discomfort, abnormal taste, tingling, mouth pain, and canker sores, along with sleepiness, fatigue, and dry mouth. Mouth-related effects usually begin within minutes of a dose and most resolve within an hour. Moistening your mouth with sips of water before dosing reduces the risk of numbness. Tell your healthcare provider if mouth effects are severe. 3
Serious cyclobenzaprine side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to cyclobenzaprine: hives; difficult breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or itching. 2,3
Stop taking cyclobenzaprine and call your doctor at once if you have: 1,2,3
- fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeats;
- chest pain or pressure, or pain spreading to your jaw or shoulder;
- sudden numbness or weakness, slurred speech, or balance problems; or
- symptoms of serotonin syndrome: agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness or twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Serious side effects, including confusion, hallucinations, and heart problems leading to falls, are more likely in older adults. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine make you sleepy?:
Yes, drowsiness is the most common side effect of the tablets, affecting up to 38% of people taking the 10 mg dose in clinical trials. This is one reason 5 mg is the usual starting dose, since it causes less drowsiness with comparable effectiveness. Analysis of trial data shows cyclobenzaprine relieves muscle spasm whether or not sedation occurs, so drowsiness is not required for it to work. 1
Does cyclobenzaprine cause constipation?:
Constipation is a known side effect, reported in 1% to 3% of people taking the immediate-release tablets and up to 3% of people taking Amrix 30 mg in clinical trials. It results from the drug's anticholinergic (drying) effects, the same mechanism behind dry mouth and blurred vision. 1,2
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Before taking this medicine
Do not use this medicine if you have used an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days. A dangerous drug interaction could occur. MAO inhibitors include isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, rasagiline, selegiline, tranylcypromine, and others.
You should not take this medicine if you are allergic to it or if you have ever had:
- a seizure disorder;
- an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia; or
- if you have suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or a sedative (such as Xanax, Valium, Fiorinal, Klonopin, and others).
Do not take this medicine to treat more than one condition at a time. If you take bupropion for depression, do not also take this medicine to quit smoking or for weight management.
Tell your doctor about all of your medical conditions and the drugs you use.
To make sure this medicine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- a head injury, seizures, or brain or spinal cord tumor;
- narrow-angle glaucoma;
- heart disease, high blood pressure, or a heart attack;
- diabetes;
- kidney or liver disease (especially cirrhosis);
- depression, bipolar disorder or other mental illness; or
- if you drink alcohol.
Some young people have thoughts about suicide when first taking an antidepressant. Your doctor will need to check your progress at regular visits while you are using this medicine. Your family or other caregivers should also be alert to changes in your mood or symptoms.
Pregnancy:
Talk to your healthcare provider if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant about the risk to your unborn baby. It is not known whether this medicine will harm an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Do not start or stop taking bupropion without your doctor's advice.
If you become pregnant during treatment, talk to your healthcare provider about registering with the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants. You can register by calling 1-844-405-6185.
Breastfeeding:
Tell your healthcare provider if you are breastfeeding or plan to breastfeed while taking this medicine. This medicine passes into breast milk, and there have been reports of seizures in breastfed infants. Talk to your healthcare provider about the best way to feed your baby during treatment with this medicine.

## Dosing Information
Usual Adult Dose of Meloxicam for Osteoarthritis:
Oral Tablets and Oral Disintegrating Tablets: -Initial dose: 7.5 mg orally once a day -Maintenance dose: 15 mg orally once a day in patients requiring additional analgesia -Maximum dose: 15 mg orally once a day Oral Capsules: -Initial dose: 5 mg orally once a day -Maintenance dose: 10 mg orally once a day in patients requiring additional analgesia -Maximum dose: 10 mg orally once a day.
Use: For the relief of signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis pain
Usual Adult Dose of Meloxicam for Rheumatoid Arthritis:
Oral Tablets and Oral Disintegrating Tablets: -Initial dose: 7.5 mg orally once a day -Maintenance dose: 15 mg orally once a day in patients requiring additional analgesia -Maximum dose: 15 mg orally once a day.
Use: For the relief of signs and symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis
Usual Adult Dose of Meloxicam IV for Pain:
- 30 mg IV bolus (over 15 seconds) once a day.
The median time to meaningful pain relief was 2 to 3 hours in clinical trials.
- A non-NSAID with a rapid onset may be used in combination with IV meloxicam.
- Some patients may not experience adequate analgesia for the first 24 hours.
- The lowest effective dose for the shortest duration possible consistent with individual treatment goals should be used.
Usual Pediatric Dose of Meloxicam for Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis:
- Oral disintegrating tablets in children 60 kg or greater: 7.5 mg orally once a day.
- Oral suspension in children 2 years and older: 0.125 mg/kg orally once a day (to a maximum dose of 7.5 mg/day).
No additional benefit has been demonstrated with doses above 7.5 mg/day. Oral formulations have not shown equivalent systemic exposure and are not considered interchangeable.
The oral disintegrating tablets should not be used in children who weigh less than 60 kg.

## Metformin dose Information
Usual Adult Metformin Dose for Diabetes Type 2:
Immediate-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally twice a day or 850 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase by 500 mg increments weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks as tolerated. Maintenance dose: 2000 mg/day in divided doses Maximum dose: 2550 mg/day. Doses above 2,000 mg may be better tolerated given 3 times
Extended-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 to 1000 mg orally once a day Dose titration: Increase in 500 mg increments weekly as tolerated Maximum dose: 2000 mg/day
Usual Pediatric Dose for Diabetes Type 2 (10 years or older):
Immediate-release tablets:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally twice a day Dose titration: Increase in 500 mg increments weekly as tolerated; daily dose should be taken in divided doses 2 to 3 times a day with meals Maximum dose: 2000 mg/day
Extended-release oral suspension:
Initial dose: 500 mg orally once a day with evening meal Dose titration: Increase in 500 mg increments weekly based on glycemic control and tolerability Maximum dose: 2000 mg/day
Renal Impairment:
- Before starting treatment, assess renal function with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)
- Do not use this medicine in patients with eGFR below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- It is not recommended to start metformin tablets in patients with eGFR between 30 to 45 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- While taking this medicine, assess the risk/benefit of continuing if eGFR falls below 45 mL/minute/1.73 m 2
- If eGFR falls below 30 mL/minute/1.73 m 2 discontinue this medication
Metformin immediate release tablets are available as 500 mg, 850 mg, and 1,000 mg tablets.
Hepatic Impairment:
Avoid use in patients with hepatic impairment.

evidence:
## What is Tirzepatide?
Tirzepatide is a once-weekly injection available as two brands: Zepbound (for weight loss, weight management, and obstructive sleep apnea) and Mounjaro (for type 2 diabetes and to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in those with type 2 diabetes at high risk).
Zepbound (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for weight loss and weight management in adults with obesity, or in overweight adults with at least one weight-related medical condition. Zepbound is also approved to treat moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity.
Mounjaro (tirzepatide) is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older to help improve blood sugar (glucose) levels, used alongside diet and exercise. It is also approved to lower the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack, or non-fatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes who are at high risk for these events.
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/ GLP-1 receptor agonist, meaning it activates two gut hormone receptors that help regulate appetite, digestion, and blood sugar. It works by reducing appetite, increasing feelings of fullness, slowing gastric emptying, boosting insulin release when blood sugar is high, and reducing glucagon secretion.
Tirzepatide is self-administered as a subcutaneous (under the skin) injection using a single-dose pen, KwikPen, or vial with syringe, and should always be used together with diet and exercise.
Tirzepatide should not be used in people with type 1 diabetes. It is not known if tirzepatide is safe in people who have had pancreatitis.

## Who should not take metoprolol?
You should not take metoprolol if you have a very slow heart rate, heart block beyond the first degree, sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, cardiogenic shock, or heart failure that is not under control.
Metoprolol is not for you if you have:
- Severe bradycardia (a very slow heart rate)
- Second-degree or third-degree heart block, which is a fault in the heart's electrical signal
- Sick sinus syndrome, unless you have a permanent pacemaker
- Cardiogenic shock, when the heart cannot pump enough blood
- Decompensated heart failure, meaning heart failure that is not stable
- An allergy to metoprolol or to any of the other ingredients in your product
Immediate-release metoprolol tartrate tablets should also not be used if your top blood pressure reading is below 100 mmHg.

## What other drugs will affect tramadol?
You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. Tramadol is broken down by two liver enzymes called CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, and medicines that block or speed up these enzymes change how much tramadol and how much of its active form are in your body. Because starting one of these medicines and stopping one both shift the balance, tell your doctor whenever you begin or finish a course of an antibiotic, antifungal medication, heart or blood pressure medication, seizure medication, or medicine to treat HIV or hepatitis C.
Many other drugs can be dangerous when used with tramadol. Tell your doctor if you also use:
- medicine for allergies, asthma, blood pressure, motion sickness, irritable bowel, or overactive bladder
- other opioid medicines
- buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, or pentazocine. These opioids work differently and can block tramadol's pain-relieving effect or bring on sudden withdrawal symptoms, so they are generally not taken with tramadol
- a benzodiazepine sedative like Valium, Klonopin, or Xanax
- sleep medicine, muscle relaxers, or other drugs that make you drowsy
- drugs that affect serotonin, such as antidepressants, stimulants, or medicine for migraines or Parkinson's disease
- carbamazepine, which is not recommended with tramadol because it can significantly reduce tramadol's pain-relieving effect and add to the risk of seizures
- digoxin or warfarin, which need extra monitoring when taken with tramadol.
This list is not complete. Other drugs may interact with tramadol, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

## Gabapentin side effects
The most common side effects of gabapentin are dizziness, drowsiness (somnolence), swelling in the hands or feet (peripheral edema), and tiredness.
Other common gabapentin side effects may include:
- unsteadiness, poor coordination, or jerky movements
- nausea or vomiting
- headache
- trouble speaking
- blurred or double vision
- tremor
- signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat
Serious side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to gabapentin: hives, difficult breathing, or swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Seek medical treatment if you have a serious drug reaction that can affect many parts of your body. Symptoms may include skin rash, fever, swollen glands, muscle aches, severe weakness, unusual bruising, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.
Tell your doctor right away if you have new or sudden changes in mood or behavior, including new or worse depression or anxiety, panic attacks, trouble sleeping, or if you feel impulsive, irritable, agitated, hostile, aggressive, restless, more active or talkative, or have thoughts about suicide or hurting yourself, while taking this medicine and after stopping it.
Gabapentin can slow or stop your breathing, especially if you have recently used an opioid medicine or alcohol. A person caring for you should seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you are hard to wake up.
Some side effects are more likely in children taking gabapentin. Call your doctor if the child has behavior changes, memory problems, trouble concentrating, or is restless, hostile, or aggressive.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- drowsiness, dizziness, or weakness
- problems with balance or muscle movement
- increased seizures
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Sertraline side effects
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%
Insomnia (trouble sleeping) | 20% | 13%
Dry mouth | 14% | 9%
Fatigue (tiredness) | 12% | 8%
Dizziness | 12% | 8%
Somnolence (sleepiness) | 11% | 6%
Tremor (shaking) | 9% | 2%
Dyspepsia (indigestion) | 8% | 4%
Agitation | 8% | 5%
Decreased appetite | 7% | 2%
Hyperhidrosis (heavy sweating) | 7% | 3%
Constipation | 6% | 4%
Decreased libido (lower sex drive) | 6% | 2%
Palpitations | 4% | 2%
Visual impairment | 4% | 2%
Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.

Montelukast helps to reduce inflammation and may be used to prevent asthma attacks in adults and children at least 2 years old.
Montelukast is also used to prevent exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (a narrowing of the air passages in the lungs due to exercise that is also known as exercise-induced asthma) in adults and children who are at least 6 years old.

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.

## How should I use levothyroxine?
Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take them before eating food. Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine:
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
- Keep using this medicine even if you feel well. It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
- You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
- This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
- Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
- Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Tablets and capsules:
Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day.
- Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it. Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
- If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken. Do not save it for later use. Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
- Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Oral solution (liquid medicine):
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
- Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
- Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
- Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast. Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away. Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
- Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Store them in their original bottle. Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Intravenous levothyroxine:
This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring:
Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable. Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7). Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change. Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.
If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering. Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

## How should I use furosemide?
Take or administer furosemide exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.
Furosemide oral tablets and liquid are taken by mouth. Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device, not a kitchen spoon.
Furosemide injection is given in a muscle, under the skin, or in a vein. A healthcare provider will give you this injection if you are unable to take the medicine by mouth.
Using subcutaneous furosemide at home:
You or your caregiver should be trained before your first dose, and you should read the Instructions for Use that comes with your prescription. Wash your hands first, and check that the liquid is clear and colorless to slightly yellow. Do not use it if you see particles or if it is cloudy or discolored.
Subcutaneous furosemide is given into the abdomen only, and you should use a different spot on the abdomen each time.
Furoscix ReadyFlow autoinjector
- Choose a site at least two inches from your belly button, avoiding skin that is broken or irritated and any scars or stretch marks. Clean it and let it dry.
- Pull the blue cap straight off, then press the device firmly against your skin and hold it there for about 10 seconds, until the yellow plunger rod stops moving and fills the viewing window.
- If you lift the device away before the window is completely yellow, you may not get the full dose. Call your healthcare provider if this happens, and do not use a second device unless you are told to.
Furoscix On-Body Infusor and Lasix ONYU Infusor
- The infusion takes about 5 hours, so plan to stay somewhere you can relax and reach a bathroom.
- Apply the device to a flat, clean, hairless area of the abdomen below the rib cage and above the belt line, and press it firmly into place. Do not remove and reapply it.
- Limit your activity while wearing it and avoid bending as much as you can. Do not exercise or do anything that might knock it off.
- Do not get the infusor wet. Do not bathe, shower, or swim while wearing it, and do not apply lotions or creams to the area where it is placed.
- Traveling by car or airplane while wearing the infusor is not recommended, and the Furoscix On-Body Infusor cannot be used in an MRI setting.
- Do not use the infusor within 12 inches of mobile phones, tablets, computers, or wireless accessories such as a remote control or Bluetooth device.
- Your healthcare provider will show you what the indicator light and alarms mean. You must use the infusor in a setting where you can detect and respond to these alarms to ensure you receive the full dose. If the device falls off, or the light blinks red, call your healthcare provider and do not reuse it.
Dispose of used autoinjectors, infusors, and cartridges in a sharps container. Do not put them in household trash and do not recycle them.
General furosemide dosing information:
Do not use more than your recommended dose. High doses of furosemide may cause irreversible hearing loss.
Doses are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
This medicine will make you urinate more often, and you may get dehydrated easily. Follow your doctor's instructions about using potassium supplements or getting enough salt and potassium in your diet.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often, and you may need other medical tests.
If you have high blood pressure, keep using furosemide even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using furosemide.

## What is the usual prednisone dosage?
The usual starting dose of prednisone for adults is 5 mg to 60 mg per day, depending on the condition being treated and how severe it is.
- There is no single standard dose. Your doctor will decide on a starting dose, then lower it in small steps to the smallest dose that still controls your condition.
- Doses for children are based on the condition rather than strictly on age or weight, and must be set by a doctor.
Short courses of prednisone for problems such as an asthma flare, gout, or a bad allergic reaction are often given as a short fixed-dose course for a few days. A dose pack steps the dose down day by day over about six days. Follow the instructions on your pack exactly, since the number of tablets changes each day.
Prednisone treatment takes one of two shapes. Some people take it for a few days or weeks for a problem that will settle, such as an asthma flare or a severe allergic reaction. Others take it every day for months or years for an ongoing condition such as rheumatoid arthritis or ulcerative colitis.
If you take prednisone long term, your doctor will settle you on a maintenance dose. This is the lowest daily dose that still keeps your condition under control, and it is reached by lowering the dose in small steps rather than all at once. Your maintenance dose is not fixed. It may need to go up for a time if your condition flares, or if you have surgery, a fever, an infection, or another serious illness, and it may come down again afterwards. Do not adjust it yourself.
How do you stop taking prednisone safely?:
If you have taken prednisone for more than a few days, your doctor will taper the dose rather than stopping it all at once. While you are taking a steroid, your adrenal glands slow down their own hormone production, and they need time to start up again. Stopping suddenly can cause extreme tiredness, weakness, body aches, upset stomach, weight loss, a craving for salt, and changes in skin color. Call your doctor if you feel unwell while your dose is being lowered or after you finish.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

## Metformin for Weight Loss: What the Research Shows
Does metformin work for weight loss?:
Yes. Metformin can lead to a modest weight loss, though results vary, and it's generally smaller amount of weight loss than what's seen with medications specifically approved for weight loss.
In the landmark Diabetes Prevention Program (DPP), a randomized controlled trial in people at high risk for diabetes, participants taking metformin lost more weight than those on placebo. Metformin patients lost 2.7% of body weight after one year, compared to 0.43% for placebo, and 2.1% after two years compared to essentially no change (0.02%) for placebo. Looking at it another way, 29% of people on metformin lost at least 5% of their starting body weight after one year, versus just 13% on placebo, a gap that held up at the two-year mark (26% vs. 14%).
Metformin is not FDA-approved for weight loss.

## How should I take carvedilol?
Take carvedilol exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose to make sure you get the best results. Do not take this medicine in larger or smaller amounts or for longer than recommended.
Take carvedilol with food.
Swallow the extended-release capsule whole and do not crush or chew it. If you have trouble swallowing, you may open the carvedilol capsule and sprinkle the medicine into a spoonful of applesauce to make swallowing easier. The applesauce should not be warm. Do not sprinkle contents on foods other than applesauce. Swallow right away without chewing. Do not save the mixture for later use. Discard the empty capsule.
Take carvedilol at the same time every day. Do not skip doses or stop taking carvedilol without first talking to your doctor. Stopping suddenly may cause chest pain or a heart attack.
If you are switched from carvedilol tablets to carvedilol extended-release capsules (Coreg CR), your daily total dose of this medicine may be higher or lower than before. Older adults may be more likely to become dizzy or feel faint when switching from tablets to extended-release capsules. Follow your doctor's instructions.
Your blood pressure will need to be checked often.
If you are being treated for high blood pressure, keep using this medication even if you feel well. High blood pressure often has no symptoms. You may need to use blood pressure medication for the rest of your life.
If you need surgery, tell the surgeon ahead of time that you are using carvedilol. You may need to stop using the medicine for a short time.
You should not stop using carvedilol suddenly. Stopping suddenly may cause chest pain or a heart attack.
Carvedilol can affect your pupils during cataract surgery. Tell your eye surgeon ahead of time that you are using this medication. Do not stop using carvedilol before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to.
Carvedilol is only part of a complete program of treatment for hypertension that may also include diet, exercise, and weight control. Follow your diet, medication, and exercise routines very closely if you are being treated for hypertension.

## Warnings
Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level. A high potassium level can cause a life-threatening change in your heart rhythm, and it often causes no symptoms until it is already high. Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.
Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.
Spironolactone should be avoided in pregnancy where possible, because it blocks male hormones and may affect how a male baby develops.

Common side effects of metformin hydrochloride tablets include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, wind (flatulence), indigestion, and headache. ## Tramadol side effects
Common side effects:
The most common side effects of tramadol are:
- dizziness or vertigo
- nausea
- constipation
- headache
- drowsiness
- vomiting
- itching.
Dry mouth is also commonly reported with the extended-release forms of tramadol.
A person's genetics can affect their response to tramadol, including their risk of side effects (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).
Serious tramadol side effects and warnings:
Tramadol may cause serious side effects, some of which may be fatal.
Tramadol can slow or stop your breathing and may be habit-forming. MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
- A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.
- Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.
You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.
Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so they can help you find the right treatment and support.
Fatal side effects can occur if you use this medicine with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing. People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time. Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death. People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk. Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).
Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. Do not stop taking tramadol suddenly without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms and uncontrolled pain (see How long does tramadol withdrawal last?).
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What other drugs affect metoprolol?
The interactions that matter most are medicines that also slow the heart and medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6, which raises metoprolol levels in your blood.
- Digoxin, clonidine, diltiazem, and verapamil. These all slow the heart's electrical signal and heart rate. Taking them with metoprolol raises the risk of a very slow heartbeat.
- Clonidine, when stopping either medicine. If you take both, the metoprolol is stopped several days before clonidine is slowly withdrawn, because beta blockers can worsen the blood pressure rebound that follows clonidine withdrawal.
- Quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and propafenone. These strong CYP2D6 blockers double the amount of metoprolol in your blood. Quinidine tripled levels of one form of metoprolol and doubled how long it lasted. Weaker CYP2D6 blockers are likely to raise levels too.
- Reserpine and MAO inhibitors. These deplete adrenaline-type chemicals and can add to metoprolol's effect, causing low blood pressure or a marked slowing of the heart.
- Epinephrine. If you need epinephrine for a severe allergic reaction, the usual dose may not work as well while you are on a beta blocker.
- Other medicines that lower blood pressure or heart rate, including fingolimod, can add to metoprolol's effect.
Tell each of your healthcare providers about all medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here.

## Warnings
Do not take spironolactone if you have a high potassium level in your blood, if you have Addison's disease (an adrenal gland disorder), or if you are taking eplerenone (Inspra), another medicine of the same type.
Spironolactone can raise your potassium to a dangerous level. Your doctor should check your potassium with a blood test within a week of you starting spironolactone or having your dose changed, and regularly after that.
Your risk of high potassium is greater if your kidneys do not work well, if you take potassium supplements or a salt substitute containing potassium, or if you take an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, an NSAID, heparin, or trimethoprim.
Do not use potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium unless your doctor has specifically told you to.
Passing too much fluid can drop your blood pressure and make your kidney function worse, especially if you are also taking an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Tell your doctor if you feel faint, or if you become unwell with vomiting or diarrhea.
If you have cirrhosis with fluid in your abdomen, spironolactone is usually started in hospital, because sudden shifts in fluid and salt can affect how your brain works.

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.

## Sertraline side effects
Common sertraline side effects:
The most common sertraline side effects are nausea, diarrhea or loose stools, trouble sleeping, dry mouth, tiredness, dizziness, sleepiness, tremor, indigestion, agitation, reduced appetite, increased sweating, and sexual problems.
The table below shows how often each side effect was reported in pooled placebo-controlled trials in 3,066 adults, compared with 2,293 people taking placebo.
Side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Nausea | 26% | 12%
Diarrhea or loose stools | 20% | 10%
Insomnia (trouble sleeping) | 20% | 13%
Dry mouth | 14% | 9%
Fatigue (tiredness) | 12% | 8%
Dizziness | 12% | 8%
Somnolence (sleepiness) | 11% | 6%
Tremor (shaking) | 9% | 2%
Dyspepsia (indigestion) | 8% | 4%
Agitation | 8% | 5%
Decreased appetite | 7% | 2%
Hyperhidrosis (heavy sweating) | 7% | 3%
Constipation | 6% | 4%
Decreased libido (lower sex drive) | 6% | 2%
Palpitations | 4% | 2%
Visual impairment | 4% | 2%
Vomiting | 4% | 1%
Some side effects were more common with particular conditions. Sleepiness was more common in depression trials, insomnia and agitation in OCD trials, constipation and agitation in panic disorder trials, tiredness in PTSD trials, and insomnia, dizziness, tiredness, dry mouth, and a general feeling of being unwell in social anxiety disorder trials. In PMDD trials, sleepiness, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and stomach pain were more common.
In these trials, 12% of people taking sertraline stopped treatment because of a side effect, compared with 4% of people taking placebo. The most common reasons for stopping were nausea (3%), diarrhea (2%), agitation (2%), and insomnia (2%).
Sexual side effects of sertraline:
SSRIs including sertraline can cause sexual problems. In men, this can mean delayed ejaculation or being unable to ejaculate, lower sex drive, and difficulty getting or keeping an erection. In women, it can mean lower sex drive and delayed orgasm or being unable to have an orgasm.
Sexual side effect | Sertraline | Placebo
Ejaculation failure (men) | 8% | 1%
Decreased libido (men) | 7% | 2%
Erectile dysfunction (men) | 4% | 1%
Ejaculation disorder (men) | 3% | 0%
Male sexual dysfunction | 2% | 0%
Decreased libido (women) | 4% | 2%
Changes in sex drive and sexual function can also be part of depression and anxiety themselves, so the timing of when symptoms started matters. These numbers may underestimate how often sexual side effects happen, because people and their providers do not always raise the subject. Tell your provider about any change in sexual function, since there may be ways to manage it.
Serious sertraline side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to sertraline: rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- signs of serotonin syndrome, which can be life threatening: agitation, hallucinations, confusion, coma or other changes in mental state, a racing heartbeat, high or low blood pressure, dizziness, heavy sweating, fever, muscle stiffness, twitching or overactive reflexes, loss of coordination, seizures, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea;
- unusual bleeding or bruising, including nosebleeds, bleeding gums, blood in vomit or stools, or black tarry stools;
- signs of a manic episode: greatly increased energy, severe trouble sleeping, racing thoughts, reckless behavior, unusually grand ideas, excessive happiness or irritability, or talking more or faster than usual;
- seizures or convulsions;
- eye pain, changes in vision, or swelling or redness in or around the eye, which can be signs of angle-closure glaucoma (a sudden rise in pressure inside the eye);
- signs of low sodium in the blood (hyponatremia): headache, trouble concentrating or thinking, memory problems, confusion, weakness, or feeling unsteady, which can lead to falls. Severe cases have caused hallucinations, fainting, seizures, coma, and death;
- fainting, chest discomfort, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of a heart rhythm problem called QTc prolongation.
Sertraline side effects in children and teenagers:
The overall pattern of side effects in 281 children and teenagers treated with sertraline was generally similar to that seen in adults. Side effects reported in at least 2% of children and teenagers, and at least twice as often as with placebo, that were not common in adults were fever, hyperkinesia (abnormally increased movement), urinary incontinence, aggression, nosebleeds, purpura (purple spots under the skin), joint pain, weight loss, muscle twitching, and anxiety.
Reduced appetite and weight loss have been seen with SSRIs, so height and weight should be monitored during treatment.
Other reported side effects:
Less common side effects reported during studies include tachycardia (fast heartbeat), tinnitus (ringing in the ears), underactive thyroid, enlarged pupils, blurred vision, blood in the stools, swelling, unsteady walking, irritability, fever, raised liver enzymes, anaphylaxis, diabetes, high cholesterol, low blood sugar, increased appetite, joint pain, muscle spasms, poor coordination, coma, convulsions, reduced alertness, numbness, lethargy, restlessness, fainting, aggression, teeth grinding, confusion, euphoric mood, hallucination, blood in the urine, milk production from the breasts, priapism (a long-lasting erection), vaginal bleeding, wheezing, yawning, hair loss, cold sweats, skin inflammation, blistering, itching, rash, hives, bleeding, high blood pressure, and flushing.
Side effects reported after sertraline came onto the market include increased clotting times, AV block, slow heartbeat, atrial arrhythmias, QTc prolongation, ventricular tachycardia including Torsade de Pointes, breast enlargement in men, raised prolactin, irregular periods, SIADH, blindness, optic neuritis, cataract, severe liver problems including hepatitis, jaundice, and liver failure with some fatal outcomes, pancreatitis, several blood disorders, angioedema, low sodium, high blood sugar, rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), lockjaw, serotonin syndrome, movement disorders including akathisia and dystonia, psychosis, bedwetting, nightmares, sudden kidney failure, pulmonary hypertension, eosinophilic pneumonia, loss of smell, photosensitivity, severe skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, spasm of blood vessels in the brain, and vasculitis.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## What is tramadol?
Tramadol is an opioid agonist that may be used to treat moderate to moderately severe chronic pain in adults, when other pain treatments such as non-opioid pain medicines do not treat your pain well enough, or you cannot tolerate them.
- Extended-release forms of tramadol may be used in adults who require around-the-clock treatment of their pain for an extended period.
- An opioid pain medicine such as tramadol can put you at risk for overdose and death. Even if you take your dose correctly as prescribed, you are at risk for opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse that can lead to death.
Brands of tramadol include ConZip, Qdolo, Ryzolt, Ultram, Ultram ER, and Ultracet. Many have been discontinued, but generic tramadol is still available.
Taking tramadol in combination with other pain-relieving medicines such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin can provide better pain relief than just taking one pain-relieving medicine by itself (see Can you take tramadol in combination with acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or aspirin?)
Tramadol first gained FDA approval on March 3, 1995. Originally, it was classified as a non-controlled substance, but it was reclassified in 2014 to Schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act with restrictions on its prescribing. Tramadol is an opioid (see Is tramadol an opioid?).
A person's genetics can affect the pain-relieving properties of tramadol (see How do genetics affect tramadol?).

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## Dosing information
Usual Adult Dose for Erosive Esophagitis:
Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day for up to 8 weeks; however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established. Maintenance of Healing of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg orally once a day. Controlled studies have been limited to 12 months of pantoprazole therapy.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease:
Parenteral: 40 mg once a day for 7 to 10 days, administered via intravenous infusion over a period of 15 minutes. Intravenous therapy should be discontinued as soon as the patient is able to resume oral therapy. Oral: 40 mg orally once a day, for short-term administration (up to 8 weeks); however an additional 8 weeks may be considered for patients who have not healed after the initial treatment. Safety and efficacy beyond 16 weeks of therapy have not been established.
Usual Adult Dose for Duodenal Ulcer:
Study (n=54) 40 mg orally once a day, dose was increased every 12 weeks by 40 mg increments to a maximum of 120 mg per day, for 28 weeks. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete duodenal ulcer healing in up to 87% and 94% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Gastric Ulcer:
40 mg orally once a day. Data have revealed that monotherapy with daily doses of 40 mg have been associated with complete gastric ulcer healing in up to 87% and 97% of patients after 4 weeks and 8 weeks respectively.
Usual Adult Dose for Helicobacter pylori Infection:
Study (n=242) - Triple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, commonly in conjunction with clarithromycin and either amoxicillin or metronidazole to eradicate Helicobacter pylori, followed with 40 mg pantoprazole orally once daily until day 28. Triple therapy has resulted in eradication rates of greater than 95%. The QUADRATE Study (n=405) - Quadruple therapy: 40 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, concomitantly with bismuth subcitrate and tetracycline, both four times daily, and metronidazole 200 mg three times daily and 400 mg at bedtime. Helicobacter Pylori eradication was achieved in 82% of patients.
Usual Adult Dose for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome:
Parenteral: 80 mg every 12 hours, administered by 15-minute infusion. Daily doses higher than 240 mg administered in equally divided doses by 15-minute infusion, or administered for more than 6 days have not been studied. Oral: 40 mg twice daily, to a maximum of 240 mg per day. Some patients have received treatment with pantoprazole for more than 2 years.
Usual Adult Dose for Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis:
Study (n=21) - Stress Ulcer bleeding prophylaxis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg twice daily, as a bolus infusion over a period of 15 minutes, to a maximum daily dose of 240 mg, divided into three equal doses. Study (n=20) - Peptic Ulcer rebleeding prophylaxis after hemostasis in the Critical Care Setting: 80 mg IV bolus, followed by continuous infusion of 8 mg/hr for 3 days, after which therapy may be continued with an oral PPI.
