## What is tamsulosin?
Tamsulosin is used to treat the symptoms of an enlarged prostate, also called benign prostatic hyperplasia or BPH. These symptoms include a weak urine stream, trouble starting to urinate, dribbling, a feeling of not emptying the bladder completely, needing to urinate often or urgently, and getting up at night to urinate.
Tamsulosin belongs to a group of medicines called alpha blockers. It works by blocking alpha-1 receptors in the prostate and bladder neck. Blocking these receptors relaxes the muscle there, which improves urine flow and eases BPH symptoms.
Tamsulosin is taken once daily, about half an hour after the same meal each day. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not crushed, chewed, or opened.
The tamsulosin brand name was Flomax, which has now been discontinued in the U.S., but generic tamsulosin is available.
Tamsulosin is not approved to treat high blood pressure, and it is not approved for use in women or children.

You may have breathing problems or withdrawal symptoms if you start or stop taking certain other medicines. ## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Prednisone FAQs
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands for about one and a quarter to one and a half days, which is why prednisone is described as short-acting compared with steroids such as dexamethasone. This is also why a course of prednisone can affect your blood sugar, your sleep, and your energy for longer than the drug is measurable in your blood.
Why has my doctor prescribed prednisone every other day?:
Alternate day dosing means taking twice your usual daily dose every other morning instead of a dose every day. It is used for people who need steroid treatment for a long time. Giving your body a day off from the steroid lets your adrenal glands recover between doses, which reduces the risk of adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, withdrawal symptoms, and slowed growth in children.
The trade-off is that your symptoms may flare a little late in the day you do not take it. Tell your doctor if this happens, since other treatment can often be added for that gap. Do not switch yourself to an every other day schedule, and do not double up on a day you were not meant to take a dose.
What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work, while prednisolone is already in the active form. For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses. Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease, and for children, because it comes in liquid forms that are easier to dose.
Does prednisone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.
Can you take ibuprofen with prednisone?:
It is usually best to avoid ibuprofen while you are taking prednisone. Ibuprofen is an NSAID, and taking an NSAID with a steroid raises the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. The same applies to naproxen, diclofenac, and regular doses of aspirin. If you need a painkiller, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you take Tylenol with prednisone?:
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) does not interact with prednisone and does not irritate the stomach, so it is generally the preferred choice for pain or fever while you are taking prednisone. Stay within the recommended daily limit on the packet and check whether any other product you take already contains acetaminophen.
Why does prednisone keep me awake?:
Prednisone acts like your body's stress hormone, which naturally peaks in the morning to help you wake up. Taking it, especially later in the day, can leave you feeling wired, restless or unable to sleep. Taking your dose in the morning often helps. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does prednisone raise blood pressure?:
It can. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which raises blood pressure in some people, particularly at higher doses or on longer courses. Your blood pressure should be checked during treatment, and your doctor may ask you to reduce salt in your diet.
What is considered a high dose of prednisone?:
There is no official cutoff, but doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low, 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate, and more than 40 mg a day as high. A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range. What matters as much as the number is how long you take it, because side effects build up over time.
Can prednisone make you tired?:
Yes. Some people feel energized on prednisone while others feel drained. Poor sleep, mood changes and muscle weakness all contribute. Tiredness that starts as your dose is being lowered, or after you stop, can be a sign that your adrenal glands have not caught up yet, so tell your doctor if it is severe or comes with dizziness, nausea, or body aches.

## How should I use levothyroxine?
Take levothyroxine exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Some brands of levothyroxine have different dosage instructions and/or recommendations of how soon you need to take them before eating food. Always check the instructions on the label.
Oral levothyroxine:
Oral levothyroxine is taken by mouth and is available as tablets, capsules, and an oral solution.
- Keep using this medicine even if you feel well. It may take 4 to 6 weeks to get the full benefit of a dose.
- You will need frequent medical tests, and your next dose may be delayed based on the results.
- This medicine can affect the results of certain medical tests. Tell any doctor who treats you that you are using this medicine.
- Tell your doctor if you have a planned surgery or dental procedure.
- Taking more than your recommended dose will not make this medicine more effective, and may cause serious side effects.
Tablets and capsules:
Take levothyroxine tablets and capsules on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast with a full glass of water. A full glass of water is important to avoid choking or gagging, because the tablet can start to break apart quickly. Take the medicine at the same time each day.
- Swallow the capsule whole and do not crush, chew, break, or open it. Tell your doctor if your child cannot swallow a capsule whole.
- If you cannot swallow a tablet whole, crush the tablet and mix it with 1 or 2 teaspoons of water; give the mixture right away by spoon or dropper and make sure all of it is taken. Do not save it for later use. Do not mix it into soy-based infant formula or other foods that can stop levothyroxine being absorbed.
- Keep each tablet or capsule in the blister pack until you are ready to take one.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Oral solution (liquid medicine):
Measure liquid medicine with the supplied measuring device (not a kitchen spoon).
- Dosages are based on weight in children and teenagers. Your child's dose may change if the child gains or loses weight.
- Your dose needs may change if you switch to a different brand, strength, or form of levothyroxine. Avoid medication errors by using only the medicine your doctor prescribes.
- Tirosint-Sol oral solution comes in single-dose ampules and can be administered 15 minutes before eating breakfast. Squeeze the liquid directly into your mouth, onto a spoon, or into a glass of water to drink right away. Use all ampules within 3 months after opening the foil pouch.
- Ermeza and Thyquidity liquids should be taken on an empty stomach, at least 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Store them in their original bottle. Use Ermeza within 90 days and Thyquidity within 8 weeks of opening the bottle.
- Store at room temperature away from moisture, heat, and light.
Intravenous levothyroxine:
This is given as an injection into a vein by a healthcare provider and should only be used to treat myxedema coma.
Blood tests, biotin, and monitoring:
Your doctor will use blood tests to check that your dose is right, usually 6 to 8 weeks after any dose change, and then every 6 to 12 months once your dose is stable. Children are tested more often, including 2 and 4 weeks after starting treatment and 2 weeks after any dose change.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you take biotin, or a multivitamin, hair, skin, or nail supplement that contains biotin (sometimes listed as vitamin B7). Biotin can interfere with thyroid blood tests and give a falsely high or falsely low result, which could lead to the wrong dose change. Stop biotin and any biotin-containing supplements at least 2 days before a thyroid blood test.
If your symptoms and blood tests still suggest an underactive thyroid even though you are on a dose that should be enough, it may be because the medicine is not being absorbed properly, doses are being missed, or another medicine is interfering. Talk to your doctor before your dose is increased.

## What happens if I overdose?
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

## What other drugs will affect hydrochlorothiazide?
Tell your doctor and pharmacist about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.
Medicines that need particular care:
- Lithium. Lithium and diuretics generally should not be taken together. Hydrochlorothiazide reduces how quickly the kidneys clear lithium, which carries a high risk of lithium toxicity.
- Cholestyramine and colestipol. These cholesterol-lowering resins bind hydrochlorothiazide in the gut and can reduce how much you absorb by up to 85 percent for cholestyramine and 43 percent for colestipol. - Corticosteroids and ACTH. Taken with hydrochlorothiazide, these increase the loss of salts from the body, particularly potassium.

- Other blood pressure medicines. The effects add together, which may be intended, but can also lower blood pressure more than expected.

MISUSE OF THIS MEDICINE CAN CAUSE ADDICTION, OVERDOSE, OR DEATH, especially in a child or other person using the medicine without a prescription. Keep this medicine where others cannot get to it. Do not take more tramadol than prescribed, as an overdose can be fatal. Selling or giving away this medicine is against the law.
- A person caring for you should give naloxone and seek emergency medical attention if you have slow breathing with long pauses, blue-colored lips, or if you find it hard to wake up. Serious breathing problems may be more likely in older adults and people who are debilitated or have wasting syndrome or chronic breathing disorders.
- Call your doctor at once if you have: noisy breathing, sighing, shallow breathing, breathing that stops during sleep a slow heart rate or weak pulse a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out seizure (convulsions) or low cortisol levels (symptoms include nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, dizziness, worsening tiredness or weakness) low sodium levels (hyponatremia). Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, or feeling sick low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, or a fast heartbeat.
Seek medical attention right away if you have symptoms of serotonin syndrome, such as agitation, hallucinations, fever, sweating, shivering, fast heart rate, muscle stiffness, twitching, loss of coordination, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea.
Seizures have been reported in patients taking tramadol. Your risk of seizures is higher if you are taking higher doses than recommended. Seizure risk is also higher in those with epilepsy or a history of seizures, and in those taking certain antidepressants, other opioids, MAO inhibitors, or other medicines that lower the seizure threshold.
You should not take tramadol if you have significant breathing problems, acute or severe asthma in a setting where you cannot be monitored, a blockage in your stomach or intestines, or if you have taken an MAO inhibitor in the past 14 days (isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue injection, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, and others). Tell your doctor before starting tramadol if you have a head injury or increased pressure inside your skull, as tramadol should be used with particular care in these situations.
Prescribers are advised not to prescribe tramadol for people who are suicidal or prone to addiction, and to use it with caution in people taking tranquilizers or antidepressants, or drinking heavily. If you are struggling with thoughts of harming yourself, or with your use of any medicine, tell your healthcare provider so they can help you find the right treatment and support.
Fatal side effects can occur if you use this medicine with alcohol, or with other drugs that cause drowsiness or slow your breathing. People taking extended-release forms of tramadol should not consume alcohol-containing beverages at the same time. Alcohol is also not advised with immediate-release forms of tramadol.
Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have occurred with tramadol, some of which caused death. People who are allergic to other opioids are at higher risk. Other hypersensitivity reactions include itching, hives, narrowing of the airways, swelling of the face and airways (angioedema), and serious skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome. Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to tramadol (symptoms include hives, difficulty breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning in your eyes, skin pain, a red or purple skin rash that spreads and causes blistering and peeling).
Tramadol may make pain worse rather than better in some people, an effect called opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Tramadol extended-release capsules and tablets may complicate a healthcare provider’s clinical assessment of an acute abdominal condition. They are not recommended for people with severe liver or severe kidney impairment.
Taking tramadol during pregnancy may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in the newborn, known as neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS).
Some people are “ultra-rapid metabolizers” of tramadol because of a variation in an enzyme called CYP2D6. Their bodies convert tramadol into its active form faster than usual, which can produce dangerously high opioid levels even at a normal dose. Life-threatening breathing problems and deaths have occurred in children for this reason, including after surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Tramadol should not be given to a child younger than 12 years old, or to anyone younger than 18 years old who has recently had surgery to remove the tonsils or adenoids. Extended-release tramadol should not be given to anyone younger than 18 years.
Tramadol may cause drowsiness or affect your ability to drive or perform hazardous tasks. Do not perform these tasks if tramadol causes confusion, mental impairment, or drowsiness.
Tramadol can cause withdrawal symptom s if stopped suddenly after being taken for a long period of time. Symptoms may include restlessness, drug craving, anxiety, and sweating. Do not stop taking tramadol suddenly without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping abruptly can cause serious withdrawal symptoms and uncontrolled pain (see How long does tramadol withdrawal last?).
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.

Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.

## Before taking this medicine
You should not use methylphenidate if you are allergic to it, or if you have:

- overactive thyroid;

## Prednisone FAQs
Is prednisone a steroid?:
Yes. Prednisone is a corticosteroid, also called a glucocorticoid. Corticosteroids are copies of hormones your adrenal glands make naturally, and they work by lowering inflammation and immune activity. They are not the same as the anabolic steroids some athletes misuse to build muscle.
How long does it take for prednisone to work?:
Prednisone starts to be absorbed within about an hour, and many people notice a difference in symptoms such as swelling, pain, or wheezing within a few hours to a day. Some conditions take several days or longer to respond. Delayed-release tablets are designed to release the medicine about four hours after you take them, so the timing of your dose matters.
How long does prednisone stay in your system?:
Prednisone and prednisolone have a half-life of about 2 to 3 hours, which means half of a dose leaves your blood in that time. Most of a single dose is out of your bloodstream within about a day.
The effect lasts longer than the drug itself. A single dose of prednisone quiets your own adrenal glands for about one and a quarter to one and a half days, which is why prednisone is described as short-acting compared with steroids such as dexamethasone. This is also why a course of prednisone can affect your blood sugar, your sleep, and your energy for longer than the drug is measurable in your blood.
Why has my doctor prescribed prednisone every other day?:
Alternate day dosing means taking twice your usual daily dose every other morning instead of a dose every day. It is used for people who need steroid treatment for a long time. Giving your body a day off from the steroid lets your adrenal glands recover between doses, which reduces the risk of adrenal suppression, Cushing's syndrome, withdrawal symptoms, and slowed growth in children.
The trade-off is that your symptoms may flare a little late in the day you do not take it. Tell your doctor if this happens, since other treatment can often be added for that gap. Do not switch yourself to an every other day schedule, and do not double up on a day you were not meant to take a dose.
What is the difference between prednisone and prednisolone?:
Prednisone has to be converted by your liver into prednisolone before it can work, while prednisolone is already in the active form. For most people the two work in a very similar way at equivalent doses. Prednisolone is often chosen for people with significant liver disease, and for children, because it comes in liquid forms that are easier to dose.
Does prednisone cause weight gain?:
Weight gain is a common side effect of prednisone. It happens for two reasons. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which adds weight quickly in the first days or weeks, and it increases appetite, which adds body fat over longer courses. It also moves fat toward the face, neck, upper back and waist. Weight from fluid usually goes once you stop, but weight from extra eating takes longer to shift.
Can you drink alcohol while taking prednisone?:
There is no direct interaction between alcohol and prednisone, but drinking is best kept to a minimum. Both irritate the stomach lining, so together they raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. Alcohol also raises blood sugar and weakens bones, and prednisone does both of these too. Ask your doctor what is reasonable for you, especially if you are on a long course.
Can you take ibuprofen with prednisone?:
It is usually best to avoid ibuprofen while you are taking prednisone. Ibuprofen is an NSAID, and taking an NSAID with a steroid raises the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding. The same applies to naproxen, diclofenac, and regular doses of aspirin. If you need a painkiller, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.
Can you take Tylenol with prednisone?:
Acetaminophen (Tylenol) does not interact with prednisone and does not irritate the stomach, so it is generally the preferred choice for pain or fever while you are taking prednisone. Stay within the recommended daily limit on the packet and check whether any other product you take already contains acetaminophen.
Why does prednisone keep me awake?:
Prednisone acts like your body's stress hormone, which naturally peaks in the morning to help you wake up. Taking it, especially later in the day, can leave you feeling wired, restless or unable to sleep. Taking your dose in the morning often helps. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does prednisone raise blood pressure?:
It can. Prednisone makes your body hold onto salt and water, which raises blood pressure in some people, particularly at higher doses or on longer courses. Your blood pressure should be checked during treatment, and your doctor may ask you to reduce salt in your diet.
What is considered a high dose of prednisone?:
There is no official cutoff, but doctors generally treat doses under 7.5 mg a day as low, 7.5 mg to 40 mg a day as moderate, and more than 40 mg a day as high. A dose of 20 mg a day sits in the moderate range. What matters as much as the number is how long you take it, because side effects build up over time.
Can prednisone make you tired?:
Yes. Some people feel energized on prednisone while others feel drained. Poor sleep, mood changes and muscle weakness all contribute. Tiredness that starts as your dose is being lowered, or after you stop, can be a sign that your adrenal glands have not caught up yet, so tell your doctor if it is severe or comes with dizziness, nausea, or body aches.

## What is the difference between hydroxyzine hydrochloride and hydroxyzine pamoate?
Hydroxyzine hydrochloride (HCl) and hydroxyzine pamoate are two salt forms of the same active medicine. Taken by mouth, FDA-approved labeling gives them the same approved uses, the same doses, the same warnings, and the same side effects.
The injection is the exception. It is a hydroxyzine HCl product; there is no pamoate injection, and it has its own approved uses, doses, and warnings.
The practical differences are:
- Form. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride comes as tablets and as an oral solution. Hydroxyzine pamoate comes as capsules.
- How they dissolve. Hydroxyzine hydrochloride is very soluble in water. Hydroxyzine pamoate is practically insoluble in water.
- How the strength is measured. Hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by the amount of hydroxyzine HCl they are equivalent to. A 25 mg pamoate capsule delivers the same amount of active medicine as a hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg tablet.
The two salts also had different brand names. Vistaril was the brand name for hydroxyzine pamoate, and Atarax was the brand name for hydroxyzine hydrochloride. Both brands have been discontinued in the United States, and hydroxyzine is now available as a generic medicine.
Is hydroxyzine pamoate stronger or longer lasting than hydroxyzine hydrochloride?:
No. You may read that hydroxyzine pamoate works better for anxiety, lasts longer, or reaches the brain more effectively than hydroxyzine hydrochloride. FDA-approved labeling does not support this.
Labeling for both salt forms states that hydroxyzine's effects are usually noticed within 15 to 30 minutes of a dose taken by mouth. Both are approved for the same three uses. Both carry the same doses, which are 50 to 100 mg four times a day for anxiety in adults, and 25 mg three or four times a day for itching. No FDA labeling describes a difference in how strongly or how long either form works.
The reason the doses match is that hydroxyzine pamoate capsules are labeled by their hydroxyzine hydrochloride equivalent. A 25 mg pamoate capsule and a 25 mg hydrochloride tablet deliver the same amount of active medicine.
If you feel that one form suits you better than the other, tell your doctor. People can respond differently to the same medicine.

## Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) dosage information
Your doctor will choose the smallest dose that controls your condition, and may adjust it over time. Follow your prescription label and do not change your dose yourself.
HCTZ dose for high blood pressure (adults):
Tablets: The starting dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once a day, which may be increased to 50 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Doses above 50 mg a day are often associated with a marked drop in blood potassium. Most people do not need more than 50 mg a day when hydrochlorothiazide is taken alongside other blood pressure medicines
Capsules: The starting dose is a hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg capsule once a day, whether taken on its own or with other blood pressure medicines. Total daily doses above 50 mg are not recommended. Capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
HCTZ dose for fluid retention (adults):
Tablets: The usual dose is hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg to 100 mg a day, taken as a single dose or split into two doses. Many people with fluid retention respond to intermittent treatment, such as taking it every other day or on 3 to 5 days each week. Excessive response and undesirable electrolyte imbalance are less likely to occur with intermittent dosing.
HCTZ dose for children for high blood pressure and fluid retention:
The usual HCTZ dose in children, for both high blood pressure and fluid retention, is 1 mg to 2 mg per kilogram of body weight (0.5 mg to 1 mg per pound) a day, given as a single dose or split into two doses.
- Infants under 6 months: may be need doses of up to 3 mg per kilogram (1.5 mg per pound) a day, given as two divided doses up to the same maximum 37.5 mg daily limit
- Infants and children under 2 years: do not exceed 37.5 mg a day
- Children 2 to 12 years: do not exceed 100 mg a day
The dose is based on your child's weight and must be worked out by their doctor.
Taking the oral suspension:
If your child has been prescribed the liquid form (oral suspension), the following applies:
- Shake the bottle well before every dose.
- Measure each dose with the oral dosing syringe. Ask your pharmacist for a syringe and a bottle adapter if you do not have them.
- Never measure a dose with a household teaspoon or tablespoon, because these do not give an accurate amount.
- Store the made-up suspension at room temperature and do not freeze it.
- Throw away any unused suspension 30 days after it was made up. The pharmacist will write this date on the bottle.
The oral suspension can be taken with or without food.
What happens if I miss a dose?:
Take the medicine as soon as you can, but skip the missed dose if it is almost time for your next dose. Do not take two doses at one time.
What happens if I overdose?:
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222.
Overdose symptoms may include nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, thirst, and muscle pain or weakness.

## What is insulin glargine?
Insulin glargine is a long-acting insulin used to treat type 1 and type 2 diabetes in certain patients to improve and maintain blood glucose levels. Insulin glargine is a man-made form of human insulin that is used once daily to provide a base level of insulin that keeps working for 24 hours or longer.
Insulin glargine is available under the brand names Lantus, Basaglar, Toujeo, Semglee, and Rezvoglar. Langlara is an interchangeable biosimilar to Lantus that was FDA-approved on May 4, 2026.
Rezvoglar, Lantus, Langlara, Semglee, and Toujeo are FDA-approved to be used for use in adult and pediatric patients with type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Basasglar is FDA-approved to be used by adults for type 2 diabetes and also for adults and pediatric patients with type 1 diabetes. In patients with type 1 diabetes, insulin glargine must be used together with a short-acting insulin.

## Before Taking
Do not take hydrocodone and acetaminophen if you have:
- Severe asthma, trouble breathing, or other lung problems
- A bowel blockage or a narrowing of the stomach or intestines
- Signs of an allergy, such as a rash
- Are allergic to any of its ingredients.

- Liver, kidney, thyroid problems
- Problems urinating
- Pancreas or gallbladder problems
- Abuse of street or prescription drugs, alcohol addiction, or mental health problems.

## How should I take potassium chloride?
Take potassium chloride exactly as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets. Your doctor may occasionally change your dose.
Read and carefully follow any Instructions for Use provided with your medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist if you do not understand these instructions.
Take potassium chloride with a full glass of water. Take potassium chloride with food or just after a meal.
Measure liquid medicine with the dosing syringe provided, or with a special dose-measuring spoon or medicine cup. If you do not have a dose-measuring device, ask your pharmacist for one.
Do not crush, chew, or suck on a tablet or capsule. Sucking on the pill could irritate your mouth or throat.
Call your doctor if you have trouble swallowing a potassium chloride capsule or tablet. You may be able to dissolve the tablet in water, or mix the medicine from a capsule with soft food. Carefully follow your doctor's instructions.
Mix the powder form of this medicine with at least 4 ounces (one-half cup) of cold water or fruit juice before taking. Drink the mixture slowly, over 5 to 10 minutes in all. To make sure you get the entire dose, add a little more water to the same glass, swirl gently and drink right away.
To be sure this medicine is helping your condition, you may need frequent blood tests. You may not notice any change in your symptoms, but your blood work will help your doctor determine how long to treat you with potassium chloride. Your heart function may need to be checked using an electrocardiograph or ECG (sometimes called an EKG). Even if you have no symptoms, tests can help your doctor determine if this medicine is effective.
Your treatment may include a special diet. Follow the diet plan created for you by your doctor or nutrition counselor. Get familiar with the list of foods you should eat or avoid to help control your condition.
Potassium-rich foods include: squash, baked potatoes (skin on), spinach, lentils, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, zucchini, kidney or navy beans, raisins, watermelon, orange juice, bananas, cantaloupe, and low-fat milk or yogurt. Consume only the daily amounts recommended by your doctor or nutrition counselor.
Some tablets are made with a shell that is not absorbed or melted in the body. Part of this shell may appear in your stool. This is normal and will not make the medicine less effective.
Store at room temperature away from moisture and heat. Keep the medication in a closed container.

## Important Information About Tramadol
Get emergency help or call 911 right away if you take too many tramadol (overdose). When you first start taking tramadol, when your dose is changed, or if you take too much (overdose), serious or life-threatening breathing problems that can lead to death may occur. Ask your healthcare provider about medicines like naloxone or nalmefene that can be used in an emergency to reverse an opioid overdose.
Taking tramadol with other opioid medicines, benzodiazepines, gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin), alcohol, or other central nervous system depressants (including street drugs) can cause severe drowsiness, decreased awareness, breathing problems, coma, and death.
Do not take tramadol with any other medicine that contains tramadol. Check the label of every pain medicine you take, as some combination products contain tramadol.
You should be given a Medication Guide each time you fill a tramadol prescription. Read it every time, even if you have taken tramadol before, because the information may have changed. Your healthcare provider or pharmacist should also go through the risks of tramadol and how to take it safely with you, and explain what to do in an emergency.
Never give anyone else your tramadol. They could die from taking it. Selling or giving away tramadol is against the law.
Store tramadol securely, out of sight and reach of children, and in a location not accessible by others, including visitors to the home.

## What happens if I overdose?
Seek emergency medical attention or call the Poison Help line at 1-800-222-1222. An overdose of acetaminophen and hydrocodone can be fatal.
Acute overdosage with hydrocodone and acetaminophen can cause respiratory depression, sleepiness progressing to near-unconsciousness or coma, floppy muscles, cold and clammy skin, constricted pupils, and, in some cases, pulmonary edema, slow heartbeat, low blood pressure, partial or complete airway obstruction, unusual snoring, and death. If the patient who has overdosed becomes very low in oxygen, pupils may become very dilated instead of constricted.
Your doctor may recommend that you get naloxone (a medicine to reverse an opioid overdose) and keep it with you at all times. A person caring for you can give the naloxone if you stop breathing or don't wake up. Your caregiver must still get emergency medical help and may need to perform CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) on you while waiting for help to arrive.
Anyone can buy naloxone from a pharmacy or local health department. Make sure any person caring for you knows where you keep naloxone and how to use it.
The first signs of an acetaminophen overdose include loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, sweating, and confusion or weakness. Later symptoms may include pain in your upper stomach, dark urine, and yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes.

## What are the side effects of hydroxyzine?
The most common side effects of hydroxyzine are drowsiness, dry mouth, and headache. These are usually mild and do not last long.
A skin rash is different. If you develop a rash while taking hydroxyzine, stop taking it and call your doctor, because a rash can be the first sign of a serious reaction.
Common side effects:
Common hydroxyzine side effects include dry mouth, headache, and drowsiness. The drowsiness is usually temporary and may go away after a few days of treatment or when the dose is lowered.
Serious side effects:
Stop taking hydroxyzine and call your doctor right away if you develop a skin rash, if a skin condition you are treating gets worse, or if you have any other sign of an allergic reaction.
In rare cases, hydroxyzine can cause a serious skin reaction called acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP). Signs include fever together with many small, shallow, pus-filled spots appearing across large areas of swollen, red skin. If you have had AGEP or another allergic reaction to hydroxyzine, you should also avoid cetirizine and levocetirizine, because a similar reaction can happen with those medicines.
Hydroxyzine has also been linked to a heart rhythm problem called QT prolongation, which can lead to a serious irregular heartbeat known as Torsade de Pointes.
Other reported side effects include:
- tremor or seizures (convulsions), which are rare and have usually happened at doses much higher than recommended
- hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)
- skin reactions including rash, hives, itching, and fixed drug eruptions, which are rashes that come back in the same spot each time the medicine is taken
- allergic reaction
Serious breathing problems have not been reported at recommended doses.
If you are given hydroxyzine by injection, tell your healthcare provider straight away about severe pain, swelling, or skin changes where the injection was given. In rare cases, the injection has caused serious damage to the surrounding tissue, including tissue death (necrosis) and gangrene, which has needed surgery to treat.
This is not a complete list of side effects, and others may happen. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to the FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.

## Sertraline FAQs
Is sertraline the same as Zoloft?:
Yes. Sertraline is the active ingredient, and Zoloft is the brand name it is sold under in the United States. Sertraline is the generic version of Zoloft, and the two contain the same medicine, sertraline hydrochloride. You may also see it written as sertraline HCl.
Is sertraline an SSRI, and how does it work?:
Yes, sertraline is an SSRI, which stands for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Nerve cells in the brain release serotonin to send signals, then reabsorb it. Sertraline blocks that reabsorption, so more serotonin stays available between nerve cells. Sertraline has very little effect on norepinephrine and dopamine, and it has no meaningful effect on adrenergic, cholinergic, GABA, dopamine, histamine, or benzodiazepine receptors, which is part of why it is described as selective.
How long does sertraline take to work?:
Sertraline levels in the blood become steady after about a week of once daily dosing, but the effect on symptoms takes longer. The trials that established sertraline ran for 6 to 12 weeks for depression, OCD, panic disorder, PTSD, and social anxiety disorder, and over three menstrual cycles for PMDD, which gives a sense of the time frame over which the benefit was measured. Because it takes time, doses are usually raised no more often than once a week, and you should keep taking sertraline even if you do not feel a change yet.
How long does sertraline stay in your system?:
Sertraline has a half-life of about 26 hours, meaning half of what is in your blood is cleared in roughly a day. At that rate, most of a dose has left your bloodstream within about 5 to 6 days. Its main breakdown product, N-desmethylsertraline, lasts longer, with a half-life of 62 to 104 hours, though it is much less active than sertraline itself. Sertraline can also cause false-positive urine screening tests for benzodiazepines for several days after you stop taking it.
Should I take sertraline in the morning or at night?:
Either is fine. Sertraline is taken once a day, in the morning or the evening, and the label does not favor one over the other. What matters more is taking it at around the same time each day. Insomnia was reported by 20% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 13% on placebo, and sleepiness by 11% compared with 6%, so some people find one timing suits them better than the other. Talk to your doctor before changing when you take it.
Does sertraline cause weight gain or weight loss?:
Reduced appetite is a common sertraline side effect, reported by 7% of adults in trials compared with 2% on placebo. Increased appetite was reported less often, in fewer than 2% of people. In children and teenagers taking sertraline for depression, there was a difference in weight change of roughly 1 kg compared with placebo over 10 weeks, representing slight weight loss on sertraline and slight gain on placebo. Around 7% of children lost more than 7% of their body weight, compared with none on placebo. In a longer 34 week extension study, weight gain was similar to what would be expected for their age. Height and weight should be monitored in younger patients. Tell your doctor about any weight change that concerns you.
Does sertraline make you tired or sleepy?:
It can. Sleepiness was reported by 11% of adults taking sertraline in trials, compared with 6% on placebo, and tiredness by 12% compared with 8%. Sertraline can also affect how clearly you think and how quickly you react, so do not drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Is sertraline a controlled substance?:
No. Sertraline is not a controlled substance. In a study comparing sertraline with alprazolam and d-amphetamine, sertraline did not produce the effects associated with a potential for misuse, such as euphoria or drug liking, that were seen with the other two medicines.
Can sertraline cause diarrhea or nausea?:
Yes, these are the two most common sertraline side effects. Nausea was reported by 26% of people taking sertraline in trials, compared with 12% on placebo, and diarrhea or loose stools by 20% compared with 10%. Nausea was also the most common reason people stopped treatment. Tell your doctor if these do not settle.
How do you stop taking sertraline safely?:
Lower the dose gradually rather than stopping all at once, and only under your doctor's guidance. Symptoms reported after stopping a serotonergic antidepressant, especially when it is stopped abruptly, include nausea, sweating, low or unstable mood, irritability, agitation, dizziness, unusual sensations such as electric shock feelings, tremor, anxiety, confusion, headache, lethargy, insomnia, hypomania, ringing in the ears, and seizures.
Can you drink alcohol while taking sertraline?:
Drinking alcohol is not recommended while you take sertraline. In healthy volunteers, sertraline did not increase the immediate effects of alcohol on thinking and coordination, but the advice for patients is still to avoid it. Separately, do not take sertraline oral solution with disulfiram, because the solution contains 12% alcohol.
Can you take sertraline while pregnant?:
That depends on your situation, and it is a decision to make with your doctor rather than on your own. Studies of first trimester use suggest no overall difference in the risk of major birth defects, but use late in pregnancy has been linked with newborn breathing problems and with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. At the same time, stopping an antidepressant during pregnancy raises the risk of depression coming back. The oral solution specifically is not recommended in pregnancy because it contains alcohol.
What are sertraline 150 mg and 200 mg capsules for?:
Sertraline capsules come in 150 mg and 200 mg only, and they are not used to start treatment. They are for people who have already been taking 100 mg or 125 mg of another sertraline product for at least a week and need a higher dose. The maximum is 200 mg a day, the same as for tablets. Capsules should be swallowed whole and not opened, crushed, or chewed. If you need to come off sertraline, the dose has to be lowered gradually using another sertraline product, because there is no capsule strength below 150 mg. Capsules are approved for depression in adults and OCD from age 6, not for panic disorder, PTSD, social anxiety disorder, or PMDD.
Does sertraline interact with warfarin?:
Yes, in two ways. Sertraline can add to warfarin's effect on bleeding risk, and both medicines bind tightly to proteins in the blood, so taking them together can raise the free level of one or both. If you take warfarin with sertraline, your INR should be monitored carefully.

## What other drugs will affect metformin?
Many drugs can interact with metformin; this includes prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. Not all possible interactions are listed here. Tell your doctor about all your current medicines and any medicine you start or stop using.
Medicines that have a carbonic anhydrase inhibiting effect like topiramate (often used for seizures or migraines), zonisamide (used for seizures), acetazolamide (used for glaucoma, altitude sickness, and other conditions), and dichlorphenamide (used for a muscle condition called periodic paralysis) can raise the risk of a rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis when taken with metformin. These medicines commonly lower a substance in your blood called bicarbonate, which your body needs to keep its acid levels balanced. If you're taking metformin along with any of these medicines, your doctor may want to monitor you more closely.
Other medicines that may increase risk of lactic acidosis. Some medicines including cimetidine (used for heartburn), ranolazine (used for chest pain/angina), dolutegravir (used to treat HIV), and vandetanib (used to treat certain thyroid cancers) can all cause metformin levels to increase. They do this by blocking the same pathway your kidneys use to clear metformin out of your system. Since higher metformin levels raise the risk of lactic acidosis, your doctor will weigh the benefits and risks before prescribing any of these together with metformin.
Insulin or other diabetes medicines that raise insulin (like sulfonylureas): Combining these with metformin can lower your blood sugar too much. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you're taking more than one diabetes medicine.
Alcohol: Drinking alcohol, especially in large amounts or regularly, can make it harder for your body to process metformin normally and raises the risk of lactic acidosis.
Contrast dye used in imaging tests (like CT scans): This type of dye can temporarily affect kidney function, which can let metformin build up in your body. Your doctor may have you stop taking metformin around the time of the test and restart it once your kidney function is confirmed to be back to normal.

## Semaglutide side effects
Common semaglutide side effects:
Common semaglutide side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, burping, gas, bloating, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, loss of appetite, diarrhea, constipation, stomach flu symptoms, low blood sugar (in people with type 2 diabetes), headache, dizziness, tiredness, hair loss, and changes in skin sensations.
Stomach or gastrointestinal side effects are common, but they tend to be mild and clear up in a few weeks and usually will not interfere with long-term treatment. Stomach side effects can be more common with higher doses.
Tips for managing stomach side effects:
Following these tips may help you manage stomach semaglutide side effects:
- Eat more slowly
- Eat smaller meals
- Choose more bland, low-fat foods (like crackers, toast, and rice)
- Avoid eating greasy, fried foods or sugar treats
- Eat foods that contain water (like soup or gelatin)
- Do not lie down right after eating
- Drink clear or ice-cold liquids
- If possible, go outside for fresh air if you feel sick to your stomach
- Ryebelsus is not recommended in patients with severe gastroparesis.
Tips for managing low blood sugar levels (hypoglycemia) side effects:
- Test blood sugar levels regularly if you are also taking diabetic medicines, including insulin or sulphonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide/glyburide, glipizide, and gliclazide) and when you increase your semaglutide dose.
- Your prescriber might reduce your dose of insulin or sulphonylureas if needed to reduce the risk of hypoglycemia
- Symptoms of low blood sugar levels include:
- Treatment for hypoglycemia
- Severe hypoglycemia may require a glucagon injection.
Serious semaglutide side effects:
Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction: hives, itching, dizziness, fast heartbeats, difficulty breathing, swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Call your doctor at once if you have:
- vision changes;
- unusual mood changes, thoughts about hurting yourself;
- pounding heartbeats or fluttering in your chest;
- a light-headed feeling, like you might pass out;
- signs of a thyroid tumor - swelling or a lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, a hoarse voice, feeling short of breath;
- symptoms of pancreatitis - severe pain in your upper stomach spreading to your back, nausea with or without vomiting, fast heart rate;
- gallbladder problems - upper stomach pain, fever, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes);
- low blood sugar - headache, hunger, weakness, sweating, confusion, irritability, dizziness, fast heart rate, or feeling jittery;
- kidney problems - swelling, urinating less, feeling tired or short of breath; or
- stomach flu symptoms - stomach cramps, vomiting, loss of appetite, diarrhea (may be watery or bloody); or severe stomach problems like severe constipation, fecal impaction, or intestinal obstruction.

Use Flonase exactly as directed on the label, or as prescribed by your doctor. Follow all directions on your prescription label and read all medication guides or instruction sheets.

## What other drugs will affect gabapentin?
Taking gabapentin with other medicines that make you drowsy or slow your breathing can cause dangerous side effects, including life-threatening breathing problems. Ask your doctor before using gabapentin with:
- opioid pain medicines such as hydrocodone, oxycodone, morphine, or buprenorphine
- sleeping pills such as zolpidem
- anxiety medicines such as lorazepam and other benzodiazepines
- muscle relaxers, sedatives, or other seizure medicines that cause drowsiness
Avoid drinking alcohol while taking gabapentin, because it can add to these effects.
Some medicines change the amount of gabapentin in your body:
- Antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium (such as Maalox) can reduce gabapentin absorption. Take gabapentin at least 2 hours after an antacid.
- Morphine can increase gabapentin levels, which may increase drowsiness and the risk of breathing problems. Your doctor may adjust your dose.
Gabapentin does not usually interact with other seizure medicines, such as phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproic acid, or phenobarbital, because it is not broken down by the liver. Your doctor can still check for interactions with your specific medicines.
Tell your doctor about all your current medicines, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products. This list does not include all possible drug interactions.

Usual Adult Bupropion Dose for Depression:
Immediate-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 100 mg orally twice a day, increase if necessary after 3 days to 100 mg orally three times a day.
- Maintenance dose: 100 mg orally three times a day
- Maximum dose: 450 mg/day in up to 4 divided doses; single doses should not exceed 150 mg
- Immediate-release tablets should be given at least 6 hours apart.
- Dose increases of the immediate-release tablet should not exceed 100 mg per day in a 3-day period.
Sustained-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increase if necessary after 3 days to 150 mg orally twice a day.
- Maintenance dose: 150 mg orally twice a day
- Maximum dose: 400 mg/day; maximum single dose should not exceed 200 mg
- Sustained-release oral tablets should be given at least 8 hours apart
Extended-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increase if necessary after 4 days to 300 mg orally once a day.
- Maintenance dose: 300 mg orally once a day
- Maximum dose: 450 mg/day
- Extended-release oral tablets should be given at least 24 hours apart
Comments:
So as not to exceed the maximum single dose of 150 mg for immediate-release tablets, a dose of 100 mg orally four times a day (using the 100 mg tablet) may be administered. Patients who are taking 300 mg/day for at least 2 weeks (OR are currently taking 450 mg/day) of any formulation may be switched to the extended-release 450 mg dose. Bupropion hydrobromide 174 mg oral tablet is equivalent to bupropion hydrochloride 150 mg. Patients should be periodically reviewed to determine the need for maintenance treatment and the appropriate dose for such treatment.
Usual Adult Bupropion Dose for Seasonal Affective Disorder:
Extended-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day in the morning, increased if necessary after 7 days to 300 mg orally once a day
- Maintenance dose: 150 to 300 mg orally once a day
- Maximum dose: 300 mg/day
Comments:
Treatment should be initiated in the autumn prior to the onset of depressive symptoms, continued through the winter season, and discontinued in early spring. If bupropion hydrochloride 300 mg orally per day is not tolerated, it should be reduced to 150 mg once a day before discontinuing treatment. Patients taking bupropion hydrochloride 300 mg orally per day during the autumn-winter season should have their dose tapered to 150 mg once a day for 2 weeks prior to discontinuation. The timing of initiation and treatment duration for seasonal affective disorder should be individualized according to the patient's historical pattern of seasonal major depressive episodes.
Usual Adult Dose for Smoking Cessation:
Sustained-release tablets:
- Initial dose: 150 mg orally once a day for 3 days, increased to 150 mg orally twice a day
- Maintenance dose: 150 mg orally twice a day
- Maximum dose: 300 mg/day; maximum single dose should not exceed 150 mg
- Duration of therapy: 7 to 12 weeks

## Hydrochlorothiazide FAQ
Does hydrochlorothiazide cause weight loss?:
Hydrochlorothiazide is not a weight loss medicine. Some people see the number on the scales drop in the first days or weeks of treatment, but this is extra fluid leaving the body rather than any loss of body fat, and it levels off. Do not take hydrochlorothiazide to lose weight.
Can you drink alcohol while taking hydrochlorothiazide?:
Alcohol can make the drop in blood pressure that happens when you stand up worse, which may leave you feeling dizzy or faint. The same applies to barbiturates and opioid pain medicines. Tell your doctor how much you drink so they can advise you.
Does hydrochlorothiazide lower your potassium?:
Yes. Hydrochlorothiazide can lower blood potassium (hypokalemia), and this is more likely at higher doses, when fluid is lost quickly, if you have severe cirrhosis, or after taking the medicine for a long time. Your doctor will check your potassium with blood tests. Tell them if you have muscle cramps, unusual weakness or tiredness, or an irregular heartbeat.
Should you eat more potassium while taking hydrochlorothiazide?:
Only if your doctor tells you to. Low potassium can sometimes be managed with potassium-rich foods, a potassium supplement, or a different type of diuretic that holds on to potassium. Do not start any of these yourself, because too much potassium can also be harmful, and some people on hydrochlorothiazide do not need extra potassium at all.
Is hydrochlorothiazide 12.5mg enough?:
For many people it is. In published trials comparing the two doses, 12.5 mg kept most of the blood pressure reduction seen with 25 mg, and low potassium was consistently less common at 12.5 mg. Starting at 12.5 mg is recommended for adults over 65. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you and may adjust it over time.

## Warnings and precautions
Do not take tamsulosin if you are allergic to tamsulosin or to any of the ingredients in the capsule.
Do not take tamsulosin with other alpha blockers such as alfuzosin (Uroxatral), doxazosin (Cardura), prazosin (Minipress), silodosin (Rapaflo), or terazosin (Hytrin).
Do not take tamsulosin 0.4 mg with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor such as ketoconazole. These medicines raise tamsulosin levels in your blood.
Tamsulosin can lower your blood pressure when you stand up, which may make you feel dizzy or faint. This is most likely when you first start taking it, when your dose changes, or when you start it again after a break. Get up slowly from sitting or lying down. Be careful driving or doing anything that needs you to be alert until you know how tamsulosin affects you.
In rare cases (probably fewer than 1 in 50,000 patients), tamsulosin can cause priapism, a painful erection that lasts a long time and is not related to sexual activity. Get medical help straight away if this happens, because without prompt treatment it can lead to permanent erectile dysfunction.
An enlarged prostate and prostate cancer can occur together. Ask your doctor about prostate cancer screening before you start tamsulosin and at regular intervals while you are taking it.
Tamsulosin can cause a problem called intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (IFIS) during cataract or glaucoma surgery. Tell your eye surgeon that you take tamsulosin or have taken it in the past, even if you stopped months ago. Do not stop taking tamsulosin before surgery unless your surgeon tells you to. If you are already booked in for cataract or glaucoma surgery, starting tamsulosin is not recommended.
If you stop taking tamsulosin for several days, talk to your doctor before starting again. You will need to restart at the 0.4 mg dose.
Many other medicines can interact with tamsulosin. Tell your doctor about everything you take, including prescription medicines, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal products.

- Notice your pain getting worse. If your pain gets worse after you take tramadol, do not take more tramadol without first talking to your doctor. Talk to your doctor if the pain you have increases, if you feel more sensitive to pain, or if you have new pain after taking tramadol.
Important Information Guiding Use in Pediatric Patients:
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 12 years of age or extended-release tramadol to anyone under 18 years.
- Do not give tramadol to a child younger than 18 years of age after surgery to remove the tonsils and/or adenoids.
- Avoid giving tramadol to children between 12 and 18 years of age who have risk factors for breathing problems. These include having recently had surgery, obstructive sleep apnea, obesity, severe lung disease, neuromuscular disease, and taking other medicines that can slow breathing.
Pregnancy:
Tramadol may harm an unborn baby and is not usually recommended during pregnancy. Use of tramadol for an extended period of time during pregnancy can cause withdrawal symptoms in your newborn baby that could be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Neonatal seizures, neonatal withdrawal syndrome, fetal death, and stillbirth have all been reported. Tramadol is also not recommended during or immediately before labor. It should only be used in pregnancy if the benefits outweigh the risks. If you are already taking tramadol and become pregnant, do not stop taking it without talking to your healthcare provider, as stopping suddenly can be harmful to you both.
Breastfeeding:
Breastfeeding is not recommended while taking tramadol, as it may harm your baby. Mothers who are ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol can have higher than expected levels of its active form in their breast milk, which can be dangerous for a breastfed infant. Carefully observe infants for increased sleepiness (more than usual), breathing difficulties, or limpness. Seek immediate medical care if you notice these signs.

## What is spironolactone?
Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) used for heart failure, high blood pressure, fluid build-up (edema) caused by liver or kidney disease, and a hormone condition called primary hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is sometimes prescribed off-label for women with acne or excessive facial hair growth (hirsutism).
Spironolactone works by blocking a hormone called aldosterone, which causes your body to pass more salt and water in your urine while keeping potassium in. This is why it is called potassium-sparing, and it is what makes spironolactone different from most other water pills, which flush potassium out.
Spironolactone also blocks androgens such as testosterone from binding to the androgen receptor, which explains several of its side effects, including breast tenderness and breast growth.
Spironolactone is FDA-approved to treat adults with:
- Heart failure (NYHA Class III-IV) with a reduced ejection fraction to help live longer, reduce swelling, and reduce the need for hospital stays. It is taken alongside other heart failure medicines rather than on its own.
- High blood pressure as an add-on treatment for people whose blood pressure is not controlled well enough by other medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of stroke and heart attack.
- Fluid build-up (edema) caused by cirrhosis of the liver when cutting back on fluid and salt has not been enough, and also for swelling caused by nephrotic syndrome (a kidney disorder) when treating the underlying disease and using other water pills have not worked well enough.
- Primary hyperaldosteronism, which is a condition where the adrenal glands make too much aldosterone. Spironolactone is used short-term to prepare for surgery, and long-term for people who are not suitable for surgery.
Spironolactone tablets come in 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg strengths. Spironolactone 25 mg is the strength most often used to start treatment. There is also a banana-flavored oral liquid for people who cannot swallow tablets. The liquid and the tablets are not interchangeable, so never switch between them without your doctor changing your dose.

## What is hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) used for?
Hydrochlorothiazide is approved to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid retention (edema) in certain patients.
High blood pressure:
HCTZ is used to manage high blood pressure (hypertension), either on its own or alongside other blood pressure medicines. Lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of fatal and non-fatal cardiovascular events, mainly strokes and heart attacks.
All three forms of hydrochlorothiazide, tablets, capsules and the oral suspension, are approved for high blood pressure in adults, and the oral suspension is also approved for children.
Fluid retention:
Hydrochlorothiazide tablets are used to treat a build-up of fluid (edema) associated with:
- congestive heart failure
- cirrhosis of the liver
- kidney conditions, including nephrotic syndrome, acute glomerulonephritis and chronic kidney failure
- treatment with corticosteroid or estrogen medicines
The HCTZ oral suspension is approved for fluid retention associated with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, and kidney disease including nephrotic syndrome, in both adults and children.
The capsules are approved for high blood pressure only, not for fluid retention.
Not all forms of HCTZ are approved for all indications and age groups.

## Metoprolol dosage
The usual starting dose is 25 mg to 100 mg once a day for extended-release metoprolol, and 100 mg a day for immediate-release metoprolol. Your dose is then adjusted at intervals of a week or longer until your blood pressure or symptoms are controlled.
Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release tablets) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 100 mg a day, as one dose or split into two | 100 mg to 450 mg a day. Doses above 450 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg a day, split into two doses | 100 mg to 400 mg a day. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
After a heart attack | 50 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours, starting 15 minutes after the last dose given into a vein. If the full intravenous dose was not tolerated, 25 mg is used. | Maintenance is 100 mg twice a day, continued for at least 3 months.
With immediate-release tablets, a once-daily dose may not keep blood pressure controlled for the full 24 hours, especially at 100 mg. Splitting the dose or taking a larger daily dose may be needed.
Metoprolol succinate (extended-release tablets and capsules) dosage for adults:
Condition | Starting dose | Usual range
High blood pressure | 25 mg to 100 mg once a day | Adjust weekly or less often. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Angina | 100 mg once a day | Increase weekly until symptoms are controlled or your heart rate slows noticeably. Doses above 400 mg a day have not been studied.
Heart failure | 25 mg once a day for two weeks, or 12.5 mg once a day in more severe heart failure | Double the dose every two weeks to the highest dose you tolerate, up to 200 mg once a day.
Kapspargo Sprinkle capsules are not suitable to start heart failure treatment if a dose below 25 mg is needed.
Metoprolol dosage for children:
Extended-release metoprolol is the only form approved for children, and only for high blood pressure in children aged 6 years and older. The starting dose is 1 mg for each kilogram of body weight once a day, up to a maximum first dose of 50 mg. Doses above 2 mg/kg, or above 200 mg a day, have not been studied. Extended-release metoprolol has not been studied in children under 6 years.
Dose adjustments:
- Liver problems. Start at a lower dose than usual and increase slowly.
- Kidney problems. No dose reduction is needed.
- Older adults. A low starting dose is generally used, because liver, kidney, and heart function are more often reduced and other medicines are more often involved.
- Switching between forms. When changing from immediate-release to extended-release metoprolol, the same total daily dose is used.

Losartan is used alone or in combination with other medications to treat high blood pressure in adults and children at least 6 years old.

Get emergency medical help if you have signs of an allergic reaction to simvastatin (hives, difficult breathing, swelling in your face or throat) or a severe skin reaction (fever, sore throat, burning eyes, skin pain, red or purple skin rash with blistering and peeling).

## Fluoxetine Dosing Information
Fluoxetine (Prozac) is taken orally, and your doctor will determine the right dose for you based on your condition, age, and response to treatment. Always follow your doctor's instructions, do not change your dose or stop taking this medicine without speaking to them first.
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD):
Adults: Treatment typically starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning. Your doctor may increase the dose after several weeks if needed. The maximum dose is 80 mg/day.
Children and adolescents (aged 8 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg or 20 mg per day. In lower-weight children, the starting dose and target dose may remain at 10 mg/day.
With all patients, the full effect of fluoxetine for depression may take 4 weeks or longer.
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD):
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 20 mg once daily in the morning and may be increased after several weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement. The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day. Full therapeutic effect may take 5 weeks or longer.
Adolescents and higher-weight children (aged 7 and older): Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after 2 weeks. Additional dose increases may be considered after several more weeks if insufficient clinical improvement is observed. The recommended dose range is 20 mg to 60 mg per day.
Lower-weight children: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day with dose increases after several more weeks if there is a lack of clinical improvement. The recommended dose range of 20 mg to 30 mg per day, although experience with daily doses greater than 20 mg is very minimal,
Bulimia Nervosa:
Adult dose: The recommended dose is 60 mg once daily in the morning. Your doctor may gradually increase your dose to this level over several days. Clinical trials showed that the 60 mg dose was effective in reducing binge-eating and purging behaviors.
Panic Disorder:
Adult dose: Treatment starts at 10 mg/day, increasing to 20 mg/day after one week. Your doctor may adjust the dose after several weeks if needed. Clinical trials used a dose range of 10 mg/day to 60 mg/day, but the most commonly used dose in clinical trials was 20 mg/day.
General Dosing Notes:
- Fluoxetine is usually taken in the morning to minimize the risk of sleep disturbances
- It may take several weeks to feel the full benefit of fluoxetine, do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first
- Your doctor will periodically reassess whether you need to continue treatment
- Older adults may need a lower dose or may take fluoxetine less frequently than younger adults
- People with liver problems may also require a lower or less frequent dose
- If you have other medical conditions or take multiple medications, your doctor may need to adjust your fluoxetine dose accordingly

## Warnings
Like all medications, Prozac carries some important warnings you should be aware of before and during treatment. Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following.
Boxed warning:
Fluoxetine carries a boxed warning, the FDA's most serious warning, regarding suicidal thoughts and behavior. Antidepressants, including fluoxetine, may increase the risk of suicidal thoughts in children, adolescents, and young adult s, particularly in the first few months of treatment or when your dose is changed. This risk was not seen in adults over 24, and adults 65 and older actually showed a reduced risk.
Anyone starting this medicine should be closely monitored for worsening mood or new or worsening suicidal thoughts, and families and caregivers should stay in regular contact with the prescriber.
Other warnings:
- Serotonin syndrome: A potentially life-threatening condition that can occur when serotonin builds up to dangerous levels. This can occur when taken alone, but is more likely when taken with other serotonergic medications. Seek emergency care immediately if you experience agitation, hallucinations, rapid heartbeat, high fever, muscle rigidity, tremor, or seizures.
- Severe allergic reactions: Stop taking this medicine and seek emergency help if you develop trouble breathing, facial swelling, hives, or blistering rash.
- Abnormal bleeding: This medicine may increase the risk of bleeding or bruising, particularly if taken with blood thinners (such as warfarin), NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen), or aspirin.
- Eye problems (angle-closure glaucoma): This medicine can cause angle-closure glaucoma with symptoms of eye pain, vision changes, or swelling around the eye in some people. An eye exam before starting treatment may be recommended for some people to assess their risk.
- Seizures: Tell your doctor if you have a history of seizures before starting this medicine, or have conditions that potentially increase your risk of seizures
- Manic episodes Fluoxetine may trigger mania, including racing thoughts, reckless behavior, drastically reduced need for sleep, and unusual bursts of energy or irritability.
- Changes in appetite or weight: Weight and appetite changes can occur, with some patients having significant weight loss. Children and adolescents should have their height and weight monitored regularly during treatment.
- Low sodium (hyponatremia): Low blood sodium levels can occur, particularly in older adults. Symptoms include headache, weakness, confusion, and difficulty concentrating.
- Heart rhythm changes (QT prolongation): Fluoxetine can affect the heart's electrical activity, potentially causing a serious and life-threatening irregular heartbeat. Seek medical attention if you experience a fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, or fainting.
- Sexual dysfunction: SSRIs, including fluoxetine, commonly affect sexual function. In men, this may include delayed or absent ejaculation or erectile problems. In women, it may include decreased libido or difficulty reaching orgasm. Talk to your doctor if this occurs, as treatment options are available.
- Drowsiness and impaired concentration: This medicine may affect your ability to think clearly, make decisions, or react quickly. Use caution when driving or operating machinery until you know how this medication affects you.
- Anxiety and Insomnia: May occur in some patients while taking this medicine.
- Blood sugar changes: People with diabetes may experience low blood sugar while taking this medicine, and high blood sugar when it is stopped. Your doctor may need to adjust your diabetes medications.

You should not take bupropion if you have seizures, an eating disorder, or suddenly stopped using alcohol, seizure medication, or sedatives. ## Before taking this medicine
You should not take cyclobenzaprine if you are allergic to it, or if you have:
- hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid);
- heart block, a heart rhythm disorder, or congestive heart failure; or
- had a recent heart attack. 1,2,3
To make sure cyclobenzaprine is safe for you, tell your doctor if you have ever had:
- liver disease; 1,2,3
- glaucoma or increased pressure in the eye; 1,2,3
- a seizure disorder (Tonmya); 3
- an enlarged prostate or problems with urination. 1,2,3
The safety and effectiveness of cyclobenzaprine tablets have not been established in children under 15 years of age. The safety and effectiveness of Tonmya and Amrix have not been established in children of any age. 1,2,3
Older adults:
Cyclobenzaprine builds up to higher levels in older adults and is more likely to cause side effects such as confusion, hallucinations, heart problems, and falls. In people 65 and older:
- Immediate-release tablets should be used only if clearly needed, starting at 5 mg and increasing slowly under medical supervision. 1
- Amrix extended-release capsules are not recommended at all, because blood levels run about 40% higher and the drug stays in the body much longer (half-life of 50 hours versus 32 hours in younger adults). 2
- Tonmya is limited to the lower 2.8 mg dose once daily at bedtime. 3
Pregnancy:
Pregnancy guidance differs by product, so check which cyclobenzaprine product you use.
Tonmya (fibromyalgia): Based on animal data, Tonmya may increase the risk of neural tube defects when used two weeks before conception and through the first trimester. Because neural tube development happens early, often before pregnancy is recognized, avoid Tonmya during this window. Your healthcare provider should do a pregnancy test before you start Tonmya, and you should use effective contraception during treatment and for two weeks after the final dose. 3
Immediate-release tablets and Amrix (muscle spasm): available data have not identified a risk of major birth defects or miscarriage, and animal studies at usual doses did not show harm to the fetus, although data are limited. These products should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. 1,2
Breastfeeding:
Small published reports suggest cyclobenzaprine passes into breast milk in low amounts, but there is no information on effects on a breastfed baby or on milk supply. Talk with your healthcare provider about the benefits of breastfeeding alongside your need for this medicine. 2,3
